title: Stock etcd Prometheus scrape fails: /metrics returns HTTP 404
body:
## Reproduction

Tigerstore main `90870876b6459334c7eddd67c0f9d184267f2eba`, built unchanged with Go 1.27.2. Three external members with client-certificate and peer TLS. Kind v0.33.0, Kubernetes v1.37.0.

Confirmed on both architectures in [run 38420832209](https://github.com/djosh34/tigerstore/actions/runs/38420832209), experiment `a503526ee91d4a816f9a0a3b3f0d82a7e4a5a984`:

- `ubuntu-24.04`, tigerstore job `115377381276`: all three members return HTTP 404.
- `ubuntu-24.04-arm`, tigerstore job `115377380689`: all three members return HTTP 404.
- Stock etcd v3.7.2 controls, jobs `115377380857` and `115377380443`: all members return HTTP 200 with Prometheus counters.

From the kind control-plane container, using the API server's etcd client certificate:

```sh
docker exec burner-control-plane curl --silent --show-error --max-time 15 \
  --cacert /etc/kubernetes/pki/external/ca.crt \
  --cert /etc/kubernetes/pki/external/client.crt \
  --key /etc/kubernetes/pki/external/client.key \
  --write-out '\n%{http_code}' https://external-etcd-1:2379/metrics
```

Repeat for members 2 and 3. The collector ran this before and after every workload phase. Tigerstore consistently returned 404; stock etcd returned counters including `grpc_server_handled_total` and Raft proposal counters.

[Collector source](https://github.com/djosh34/tigerstore/blob/a503526ee91d4a816f9a0a3b3f0d82a7e4a5a984/experiments/kube-burner/metrics.py), [per-run summary](https://github.com/djosh34/tigerstore/tree/292f36bfdcbb16aa2aa3d68e6a71ca46b8da97b9/evidence/kube-burner/workload-pilot-38420832209/summary), and [complete raw evidence archive](https://github.com/djosh34/tigerstore/blob/292f36bfdcbb16aa2aa3d68e6a71ca46b8da97b9/evidence/kube-burner/workload-pilot-38420832209/raw.tar.gz). Each run's `before/snapshot.json` and `after/snapshot.json` retain the commands, HTTP codes and collection times; `external-etcd-N.prom` retains the response body.

## Impact and scope

This breaks the stock etcd Prometheus scrape and prevents reporting tigerstore-native RPC throughput for the requested #50 Kubernetes comparison. The comparison instead reports API-server-observed storage RPC rates and actual server process CPU from `/proc`, explicitly labelled. Missing server counters are not zero.

This is an observability compatibility gap, not a demonstrated Kubernetes request failure. All kube-burner phases exited successfully and deleted their run-owned objects on both stores in this pilot. Current design documents `/health` and `/version`, not `/metrics`; this issue does not claim metrics were already implemented or required by kube-apiserver itself. Filed under #48 per the instruction to report confirmed tigerstore-only failures during this comparison. No product change is included.

title: Answer Maintenance.Alarm with no alarms, so etcdctl endpoint health passes
body:
Part of #48. This resolves bug #92; I close #92 by hand after the merge.

`etcdctl endpoint health` reads a key and then lists the alarms. Tigerstore answered `Maintenance/Alarm` with Unimplemented, so every endpoint was reported unhealthy. That blocked kind from booting on tigerstore, while stock etcd v3.7.2 passed.

**What Alarm does now** (`internal/server/rpc.go`):
- Tigerstore raises no alarms. It has no space quota, a full or failing disk stops the node, and a corrupt log keeps the node from starting. So no running node ever has NOSPACE or CORRUPT.
- etcd v3.7.2 passes every alarm request through Raft (`EtcdServer.Alarm` calls `raftRequest`). Here a linearizable read stands in, so the answer is linearizable and its header carries the current revision.
- GET (any type), DEACTIVATE, and ACTIVATE of NONE all return no alarms. That is what etcd's `AlarmStore` and applier return when no alarm is active.
- Activating NOSPACE or CORRUPT by hand would make etcd refuse writes, and tigerstore does not support it. It answers Unimplemented with a message that says so.

**Tests:**
- `TestAlarm` covers GET, GET of NOSPACE, DEACTIVATE and ACTIVATE of NONE on a follower, checking for no alarms and a header at or past the last write. It also covers Unimplemented for ACTIVATE of NOSPACE.
- The smoke job now runs `etcdctl endpoint health` against all three nodes, and checks that `etcdctl alarm list` prints nothing.
- docs/design.md has an Alarm entry, and Alarm is gone from the Unimplemented list.

**Ran locally** (`GOFLAGS=-p=2 GOMEMLIMIT=2GiB`): `TestAlarm`, golangci-lint on server (0 issues), shellcheck, and `scripts/smoke.sh`, which passed with etcdctl 3.5.17. CI runs it with v3.7.2.

Server code changed: this adds one method table entry and no hot-path code. The bench run against main and etcd v3.7.2 is started, and its numbers will be posted here.

title: etcdctl endpoint health fails because Maintenance.Alarm is unimplemented
body:
## Reproduction

Tigerstore main `90870876b6459334c7eddd67c0f9d184267f2eba`, built with Go 1.27.2, three members with client-certificate TLS and peer TLS. Stock client `etcdctl v3.7.2`. No product patches.

Confirmed independently on both free runner types in [run 38419020116](https://github.com/djosh34/tigerstore/actions/runs/38419020116):

- `ubuntu-24.04`, job `115371064715`, failed.
- `ubuntu-24.04-arm`, job `115371065453`, failed with the same error.
- Stock etcd v3.7.2 jobs `115371066414` and `115371065273` passed the identical command and then booted kind v0.33.0 with Kubernetes v1.37.0.

From experiment commit `116fab403d088d715b7f661db8e1703438747ef0`, the [boot script](https://github.com/djosh34/tigerstore/blob/116fab403d088d715b7f661db8e1703438747ef0/experiments/kube-burner/boot.sh) creates the certificates and members. It runs:

```sh
docker exec external-etcd-1 /bin-etcd/etcdctl \
  --endpoints https://external-etcd-1:2379,https://external-etcd-2:2379,https://external-etcd-3:2379 \
  --cacert /certs/ca.crt --cert /certs/client.crt --key /certs/client.key \
  --command-timeout=10s endpoint health
```

Expected: the healthy cluster returns successful health checks, as stock etcd does.

Actual: exit 1 on every attempt. Each endpoint answers:

```text
method: /etcdserverpb.Maintenance/Alarm
rpc error: code = Unimplemented desc = method Alarm not implemented
https://external-etcd-1:2379 is unhealthy: failed to commit proposal: Unable to fetch the alarm list
Error: unhealthy cluster
```

[Permanent logs, versions, binary hashes and container commands for all four jobs](https://github.com/djosh34/tigerstore/tree/cfd3b2e/evidence/kube-burner/pilot-38419020116). The `boot.log` files contain all retries, not a selected excerpt.

## Scope

This is an operator-tool compatibility failure, not evidence that Kubernetes itself failed to boot. The experiment initially stopped before kind on this check. `docs/design.md` explicitly leaves Alarm unimplemented, but that also breaks the stock health command. Filed under #48 as requested for tigerstore-only failures in the Kubernetes comparison.

The subsequent experiment retains this command's output and exit status, but gates readiness on linearizable reads for both stores. That permits the Kubernetes test to proceed without changing product code or claiming this bug is fixed.

title: Fix sim liveness bound for gray faults that outlast healing
body:
Part of #47. This resolves bug #81; I close #81 by hand after the merge.

## Cause

This is a checker bound error, not a node or Raft defect. I reproduced the failure on `origin/main` at `36eda3c`, then used temporary prints around simulator events, disk jobs, message delivery, and each node's leader, term, and applied index. The prints are not in this PR.

The issue's guessed network delay is not the full cause. The guaranteed gray network period ends at 20,970.985 ms, but a simulated gray disk job remains in flight until 22,701.346 ms. Healing only shortens explicitly stalled disk jobs. It does not cancel the delay of a gray job already in flight.

| Virtual time in ms | Traced event |
| ---: | --- |
| 19,891.554 | Node 1 starts a gray disk job, scheduled to finish at 22,701.346. The job has no entries or hard state. Its simulated storage delay blocks later jobs. |
| 20,000.000 | Scheduled healing. Node 1's disk job is still in flight. |
| 20,247.730 | Node 1 reaches term 5 after nodes 2 and 3 grant its pre-votes. There is no leader yet. Its term-5 hard state waits behind the gray job. |
| 20,970.985 | Node 3 wins term 4 with node 2. Its first append to gray node 1 drops and ends the guaranteed gray network period. |
| 22,701.346 | The gray disk job completes. Node 1 starts the queued jobs, including its term-5 hard state. |
| 22,702.239 | That hard state becomes durable. Node 1 releases held peer messages. |
| 22,702.337 | Node 3 receives the delayed term-5 vote request. CheckQuorum ignores it while the leader lease is valid. |
| 22,702.455 | Node 3 receives node 1's delayed, rejected term-5 pre-vote response and steps down. |
| 24,148 | The original checker counts a call that gets "no leader". |
| 24,169.682 | All three nodes follow node 3 in term 6. |

Raft's `Step` treats a rejected pre-vote response with a higher term as a term update. CheckQuorum's lease protection applies to vote requests, not this response. Raft's async storage path also waits for persistence before sending vote and append responses. Our additional gate holds every peer message while a term or vote change is not durable. Releasing those messages early would break the durability rule in `docs/design.md`.

The term-5 election started before the term-4 leader existed. The gray storage delay kept that term from reaching the other nodes until 2.7 s after scheduled healing. The cluster was not fault-free at 20 s, so that is the wrong point from which to allow four seconds for recovery.

## Change

Start the existing recovery allowance after the last actual gray fault effect that survives scheduled healing. Track both the guaranteed append drop and completion of an already-slowed gray disk job. A healthy completion, a canceled job from a crashed node, or a later election cannot move the bound. Preserve the existing fenced-node and late-stop rules. Extend the client phase when needed so there are at least three seconds of calls under the rule.

No node, Raft, or persistence behavior changes. `docs/design.md` states the corrected rule and records the trace. Every durability rule stays in place.

For this seed the bound is now 26,701.346 ms. The named regression also requires definite answers from 24,200 ms, before that general bound. It checks 3,130 such answers and runs the independent durability, revision, and watch checkers. The bound tests cover gray disk completions, canceled completions, healthy completions, delayed append drops, and continued client coverage.

Restoring the original 24 s bound in a temporary test reproduces the exact original failure with trace hash `65835d82593e70b9`. The corrected run has the same hash. Only the verdict changes, not the cluster's behavior.

## Checks run

Every local Go command used `GOFLAGS=-p=2 GOMEMLIMIT=2GiB`. Tests ran one at a time with `-parallel 2`. Only `internal/sim` was tested or linted locally.

- Reproduced the failing command before the change: `go test ./internal/sim/ -parallel 2 -run 'TestSeeds$' -args -sim.seed=745672193 -sim.seeds=1`.
- The same failing-seed command passes after the change.
- `go test ./internal/sim/ -parallel 2 -run 'TestGray(HealingSeed|FsyncRecoveryBound|AppendRecoveryBound)$' -v`.
- `go test ./internal/sim/ -parallel 2`, including the final version.
- `go test ./internal/sim/ -parallel 2 -run 'TestSeeds$' -args -sim.seed=745672193 -sim.seeds=64`.
- `go test ./internal/sim/ -parallel 2 -run 'TestSeeds$' -args -sim.seed=1 -sim.seeds=64`.
- Single-seed `TestSeeds` runs for the older liveness seeds `721530481` and `714720575`.
- `GOMAXPROCS=1 go test ./internal/sim/ -parallel 2 -count=1 -run 'TestGrayHealingSeed$' -v`, with the same trace hash.
- A temporary test restored the original bound and confirmed the original failure and unchanged trace hash. It was removed.
- `golangci-lint run ./internal/sim/...`: 0 issues.
- `git diff --check`.

CI runs the other packages. Do not merge this PR as part of this task.

title: Stress test of large values at real ticks, with logs of where commit time goes
body:
Part of #88.

#88 is a leader commit watchdog that fired during 1.5 MiB writes in `TestLargeValues` at 10 ms ticks. Its cause is not known. This PR adds the test the issue asks for and logs that show where the time goes when it fails. It does not fix a cause, because none has been found yet.

**Test.** `TestLargeValuesAtRealTicks` runs a 3-node cluster with a real node's 100 ms ticks. A client on every node writes values near the request limit in a loop. A new core setting, `CommitStallElections`, is set to 1 in this test. So a leader whose entry waits one election timeout (1 s) to commit stops itself, and the test fails with `core.ErrCommitStalled` at cleanup. A failed put fails it too. The default stays at three election timeouts.

The test is skipped unless `TIGERSTORE_STRESS` sets a duration. With no snapshots yet, every value stays in each node's memory: about 63 puts/s of 1.5 MiB, roughly 1 GB per node over 10 s. A new `stress` job in ci runs it 20 times for 10 s each, without `-race`, and `ci` requires it.

**Logs.** A node now logs:
- a log write (append plus fsync) that took longer than one tick, with its entries and bytes;
- each leader change, with the term;
- at most once a second per peer, the messages that waited over 100 ms in their peer queue, with the longest wait and the last message's type and size.

The test cluster prefixes every node and peer log line with the node ID and now passes the peer a logger, which it did not before.

**Run locally** (`GOFLAGS=-p=2 GOMEMLIMIT=2GiB`, `-parallel 2`): golangci-lint on core, node, peer and server (0 issues); `go test` of core, node, peer and server; `TIGERSTORE_STRESS=3s` once, with 189 puts and none failed. The 20-run job runs in CI only.

**Hot path.** Each peer message now takes a `time.Now()` when it is queued. Node and peer code changed, and server code only in tests. The bench workflow will run put and txn against main and etcd v3.7.2, and the numbers will be posted here.

title: Range answers encoded from the index's values; LIST benchmarks
body:
Part of #50: the read path, the bulk of Kubernetes' load.

**What changes:**

- **mvcc:** `Store.RangeKVs` answers a range as one slice of `mvcc.KV` values (key, value, revisions, lease), the index's own slices, instead of a `*mvccpb.KeyValue` per key. Filtering, sorting, the limit and `keys_only` are unchanged, now on values. `Range` (transactions, tests, simulator) builds its message from that result.
- **core:** a `core.Request` with `Compact` set gets its range answer as `Reply.Range`, with the term in `Reply.Term`, and no `RangeResponse`.
- **server:** Range calls are admitted as compact. The connection writer encodes the `RangeResponse` itself (`appendRangeReply`): it computes the exact size, writes the header, each KeyValue and `more`/`count`, and copies the values once into the reply. `TestRangeReplyEncoding` compares it byte for byte with protobuf's encoding on 2,000 random results, including negative leases and counts, empty keys and values, and `more`.
- **Range requests** are decoded with the field-by-field decoder from #80 (`DecodeAlias`), not `proto.Unmarshal`.
- **Batching:** linearizable reads were already batched into one ReadIndex per committer turn, on leader and followers (`core.requestReads`). This PR does not change that.
- **Benchmarks:** loadgen gets a `list` workload. It is a LIST of one of 100 namespaces, 1,000 keys each, in pages of 500 (`-page`). Each answer must carry the count of 1,000 and a full page of the namespace's keys in order, with values of the size put. `bench/run.sh` preloads 100,000 keys for `list-1k` and runs it at 2 connections × 16 streams. At the default 1,536 streams, etcd v3.7.2 lost its leader 322 times ([run 38410562311](https://github.com/djosh34/tigerstore/actions/runs/38410562311)).

**Range against main and etcd v3.7.2:** [run 38410562311](https://github.com/djosh34/tigerstore/actions/runs/38410562311), `bench` workflow, free `ubuntu-24.04-arm` runner, barriers on, generator CPU 3, leader CPU 0, followers CPUs 1 and 2. 5 repetitions back to back, 1 KiB values, linearizable point reads, every stream busy (6 × 256). Main `aa1e39c`, this PR `c1a2c43`:

| Store | reads/s (median, range) | Server CPU us/read (all nodes) | Leader cores |
|---|---|---|---|
| etcd v3.7.2 | 7,367 (7,243 to 7,609) | 136.7 | 1.00 |
| main | 169,834 (168,234 to 173,129) | 6.1 | 1.00 |
| this PR | 189,466 (188,917 to 192,963) | 5.4 | 1.00 |

That is +11.6% reads/s and −11% server CPU per read against main, with the leader's core saturated. LIST numbers will follow in a comment.

**Local:** golangci-lint, `go test -race -short` of server, core and mvcc, the difftest against etcd v3.7.2's recorded answers (which covers range options, sorts, limits, counts, revisions and keys-only), and 32 simulator seeds pass.

title: Leader commit watchdog fires during 1.5 MiB writes (TestLargeValues)
body:
`internal/server` `TestLargeValues` stopped its leader with `core.ErrCommitStalled` ("the leader's entries stopped committing") in two CI runs:

- main `8ebbd31`, [run 38389726477](https://github.com/djosh34/tigerstore/actions/runs/38389726477): `--- FAIL: TestLargeValues (0.84s)`, `node 1: core: the leader's entries stopped committing`, during cleanup.
- #86 `66ff781`, [run 38404901240](https://github.com/djosh34/tigerstore/actions/runs/38404901240/job/115321849004): the same error, after Put retries failed.

**Expected:** a 3-node cluster on loopback commits four 1.5 MiB puts without a leader entry waiting three election timeouts. **Actual:** with the test cluster's 10 ms ticks, an entry of the leader waited past 300 ms (`CommitStallTicks` × `ElectionTicks` × 10 ms), so the commit watchdog stopped the leader.

**Guessed cause, not proven:** slow fsyncs of 1.5 MiB appends on a shared runner's disk, on the followers or the leader. The logs record no fsync spans, peer delays or term changes. The watchdog measures the oldest outstanding leader entry, not the total time of the four writes, so four writes adding up to 300 ms do not by themselves explain it. Other candidates: a heartbeat or append held behind a large frame on a peer connection, a follower's committer delayed by a large apply, or Go scheduling on a loaded runner.

**Mitigation, not a fix:** #87 runs the test with 50 ms ticks (watchdog 1.5 s). Real nodes use 100 ms ticks (`cmd/tigerstore/main.go`), a 3 s watchdog.

**A test that would reproduce it at the real tick rate:** the same cluster with 100 ms ticks, writing near-limit values in a loop from several clients on every node for 30 s. It should fail if any leader entry waits more than one election timeout (1 s) to commit, rather than relying on the 3 s watchdog. It should record, per node, each append's fsync span, the peer send-queue wait for append and heartbeat messages, and term changes, so a failure names its cause. Run it in CI as its own job, repeated (for example `-count=20`).

title: TestLargeValues runs with 50 ms ticks
body:
Part of #50, whose CI this flake fails.

`internal/server` `TestLargeValues` failed with "the leader's entries stopped committing" on main `8ebbd31` ([run 38389726477](https://github.com/djosh34/tigerstore/actions/runs/38389726477)) and on #86 ([run 38404901240](https://github.com/djosh34/tigerstore/actions/runs/38404901240/job/115321849004)). With the test cluster's 10 ms ticks, the leader's commit watchdog (three election timeouts) fires after 300 ms, and four 1.5 MiB writes on a shared runner's disk can take that long. The cause is a guess from the error and the timing; the test does not log fsync times. The test now runs with 50 ms ticks, so the watchdog fires after 1.5 s, as #78 did for `TestStalledPeerLinkKeepsQuorum`. It passes locally with `-race`.

title: Lean load generator and a benchmark workflow
body:
Part of #50, its first Done-when line: a lean load generator, and a benchmark workflow that measures every speed PR with a generator that is not the bottleneck.

**Where the code comes from.** `cmd/loadgen`, `cmd/benchreport` and `bench/` are the paused load-generator worker's uncommitted code. I fixed the defects that the [pre-work review on #50](https://github.com/djosh34/tigerstore/issues/50) listed:

- Connections use TLS 1.3 with h2 and client certificates (`-cacert`, `-cert`, `-key`). Before, they were plain text.
- Latency covers every request that arrived in the window, from its scheduled send time, however late it completes. `cohort` and `cohort_failed` count those requests. Before, only completions inside the window were sampled.
- A unary call succeeds only with exactly one response message. Empty or duplicate responses no longer count.
- A result carries `valid`. Any request error, unfinished phase, failed CPU sample or missing `-pids` makes it false, and `benchreport` refuses invalid results instead of reporting zeros.
- Values are disjoint windows of random bytes, so adjacent values no longer share data.
- `bench/run.sh` starts every run on a fresh cluster directory, and `bench/cluster.sh` writes the pids before it waits, so a failed start is cleaned up.

**What else is new:**

- `bench/cluster.sh` runs etcd or tigerstore with client and peer TLS. After the election it asks `etcdctl endpoint status` for the leader and pins every thread of the leader's process to the first CPU list and the followers to the others. It records the placement next to each result.
- `bench/run.sh` runs named targets. Target `x` runs `$BINS/x`, as etcd if the name is etcd, so etcd, a baseline build and a candidate build run back to back, in reversed order on even repetitions. The generator drives the leader.
- `.github/workflows/bench.yml` (`workflow_dispatch` only) takes a candidate ref, a baseline ref, benchmarks, modes and repetitions (default 5). It runs one job per benchmark on `ubuntu-24.04-arm`. Each job installs etcd v3.7.2 with a sha256 check, remounts the root filesystem with `barrier=1` and checks it, and records the runner, commits and layout (generator CPU 3, leader CPU 0, followers CPUs 1 and 2). The report goes to the job summary and the raw results to an artifact.
- `.golangci.yml` sets exhaustive's `default-signifies-exhaustive`. The generator's switches over protobuf numbers and HTTP/2 settings have a default case, as the paused code expected.

Open beyond this PR on #50's second Done-when line: the 0/1/5/10 ms node delays, etcd's own benchmark tool as a second view, and a labelled host run.

**Trial run** of the workflow on this branch, through a temporary push trigger that is removed again: [run 38398789333](https://github.com/djosh34/tigerstore/actions/runs/38398789333). Main against itself and etcd v3.7.2, 3 repetitions, max mode only (6 connections × 256 streams):

| Benchmark | Store | ops/s (median, range) | p50 / p99 ms | Leader / follower CPU us/op | Generator CPU us/op |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| put-1k | etcd | 4,909 (4,174 to 4,966) | 305 / 581 | 180.7 / 24.7 / 24.2 | 17.8 |
| put-1k | main | 91,818 (85,243 to 93,236) | 16.3 / 36.3 | 8.6 / 3.4 / 3.2 | 2.4 |
| put-1k | main again | 90,205 (90,174 to 93,512) | 16.6 / 33.4 | 8.7 / 3.4 / 3.2 | 2.3 |
| txn-1k | etcd | 4,109 (3,963 to 4,118) | 370 / 732 | 214.2 / 31.8 / 29.7 | 18.8 |
| txn-1k | main | 53,210 (52,583 to 53,683) | 27.2 / 63.3 | 15.9 / 5.8 / 5.6 | 2.4 |
| txn-1k | main again | 53,547 (53,285 to 54,131) | 27.2 / 60.4 | 16.0 / 5.8 / 5.6 | 2.4 |

The generator used 0.22 of its core at about 92k Put/s, so it had CPU to spare. That it was no bottleneck at all is a guess: no matched run with more connections or streams checked for a stream, window or connection limit. "p50 / p99" at max is the closed-loop latency, about streams divided by throughput, not a latency at a given load. The leader CPU column is the first entry of `server_cpu_us_per_op_by_node`. The "main again" rows are the candidate slot of the same commit; they show the spread between identical builds. Rows are medians of per-run statistics.

Local: golangci-lint, `go test -short ./cmd/...`, a TLS functional run of Put and Txn against a local cluster, and `bench/cluster.sh` start/stop with placement for both stores pass.


CI: no simulator seed failed in this PR's runs. The first run on `66ff781` failed `internal/server` `TestLargeValues` ("the leader's entries stopped committing"), which this PR does not touch and which also failed on main `8ebbd31`; #87 addresses it. The rerun of that job passed, which shows only that the rerun passed.

title: Peer tests hold their ports open until the transports start
body:
Part of #50, whose CI this race can fail.

The Opus review of #78 pointed out that `internal/peer` has the same close-then-listen race that #78 fixed in the server tests (`bind: address already in use` when another process takes a port between `freeAddr` closing it and `Start` listening on it). The peer tests now open their listeners first and pass them through `Config.Listener` (added in #78). The restart in `TestReconnect`-style code listens on the same port again, retrying for up to 5 s.

`go test -race ./internal/peer/`, `go vet -tags planted` and golangci-lint pass locally. Test-only change.

title: Read the client socket at most once per committer turn
body:
Part of #50.

The leader CPU profile on #77 had `Syscall6` at 41% flat, most of it the connection readers' socket reads and the writers' TLS writes. Sol's last run measured 0.78 read and 0.37 write syscalls per Put on the leader at 256 clients; etcd made 0.39 and 4.08.

The reader read the socket as soon as it had handed a batch to the node, so every burst of requests cost a read. Now it waits, but only before a read that would go to the socket:

- After `SubmitBatch`, the connection is marked `untaken`. The committer calls the new `Completer.Taken` when it takes the batch.
- Before a socket read, `awaitTaken` waits for that signal, unless the next frame is already buffered whole. Buffered frames, and so the next batch, are still read at once. The requests that arrive while the committer works then come in with one read.
- The reader therefore reads the socket at most once per committer turn. The committer clocks it the way it clocks batches, with no timer. A lone request still goes through at once: an idle committer takes its batch right away.
- If the node stops, the wait ends and the writer fails the calls the node held, as before.

Cost: pings, resets and window updates from a client that has an untaken batch wait for at most one committer turn. Before, a reader also stopped reading while its batch waited for a full inbox.

No benchmark yet. Sol's helper will run this against main with the lean generator; the expected effect is fewer read syscalls and less leader CPU per Put.

Tests: `go test -race -short` of server and node (including `TestNodeStopsUnderLoad`) and golangci-lint pass locally.

title: Simulator seed 736998125: cold restart ends before the follower learns the last commit
body:
Seed 736998125 fails `TestSeeds` on main `e1fd889`. It came up in `sim (3)` of [run 38367998279](https://github.com/djosh34/tigerstore/actions/runs/38367998279/job/115198272785) on #75, which does not change this path.

```
go test ./internal/sim/ -run 'TestSeeds$' -args -sim.seed=736998125 -sim.seeds=1
seed 736998125: erasing node 3 at 17821 ms: the two restarted nodes did not converge: applied 112 and 111
```

**Expected:** both nodes of the cold restart apply the same entries. **Actual:** one is a single entry behind when the 6 s window ends.

Cause, traced on main: in the cold restart, the leader proposed a lease expiry as entry 112 at 5,998 ms and committed it at 5,999 ms. The follower learned the commit 1 ms after the window ended. It is a checker bound, not lost data. #78 fixes it with one extra second and the regression test `TestColdRestartWaitsForLastCommit`.

title: Simulator seed 745672193: no leader 4,148 ms after healing
body:
Seed 745672193 fails `TestSeeds` on main `e1fd889`. It came up in `sim (3)` of [run 38372335474](https://github.com/djosh34/tigerstore/actions/runs/38372335474/job/115212131105) on #78, which does not change this path.

```
go test ./internal/sim/ -run 'TestSeeds$' -args -sim.seed=745672193 -sim.seeds=1
seed 745672193: liveness: client 1 call at 24148 ms, 4148 ms after healing, failed: rpc error: code = Unavailable desc = etcdserver: no leader
```

**Expected:** every call 4 s or more after healing gets a definite answer. **Actual:** a call at 4,148 ms after healing gets "no leader".

Leadership after healing at 20,000 ms, traced with a throwaway print of each node's leader and term on main:

| ms | Event |
| ---: | --- |
| 20,247 | node 1 at term 5, no leader, applied 44 |
| 20,970 | node 3 leads term 4, applied 44; node 2 follows |
| 22,702 | node 3 steps down to term 5, applied 58 |
| 23,800 | node 2 at term 5 |
| 24,169 | node 3 leads term 6; all three follow |

Node 1 went into the fault-free period at term 5 with a shorter log. At 22,702 ms, 2.7 s after healing, the leader learned term 5 and stepped down. The next election ended 21 ms after the failing call. This is the case `liveFrom` already describes for seed 721530481 ("a node that comes out of the faults with a higher term and a shorter log can then make the new leader step down once"). Here the step-down came 1.7 s after the leader was elected, not at once.

My guess at the delay, not proven: node 1 was the gray node of the guaranteed gray period, which may last past healing until it loses an append. So its term reached the leader only once that ended. If so, the liveness rule should start from the end of that gray period, as it does from `lateStopAt` for a node that stops after healing. Whether this is only the checker's bound or a real liveness problem is open.

title: Every write in wire form, applied without copying values
body:
Part of #50. Stacked on #79; the base becomes `main` as the stack merges.

#77 kept Puts in wire form and applied them in place. Kubernetes writes are transactions (compare the mod revision, then put, else range), and those still went through a marshal into the entry and a `proto.Unmarshal` at apply on every replica. That apply copied every key and value, so transaction values sat in memory twice: once in the log, once in the index. This PR closes that gap for every write.

- **`core.UnmarshalAlias`** decodes like `proto.Unmarshal`, but bytes fields are clipped slices of the input instead of copies. It walks the wire format with protowire and sets fields through protoreflect, so protobuf's rules hold without hand-written code per message. The last scalar wins. A repeated message field appends. A singular message field or oneof member that comes again merges into the first, and another oneof member replaces it. Unknown fields and fields of the wrong wire type are kept as unknown. Malformed input fails. `TestUnmarshalAliasMatchesProtobuf` compares it with `proto.Unmarshal` (`proto.Equal`, error or not) on 3,000 random transactions with every compare and operation kind, nested transactions, concatenations of two encodings (which protobuf merges), unknown and mistyped fields, and random truncations. `TestUnmarshalAliasShares` checks that values are slices of the input.
- **Frontend.** The reader decodes every batched request (Range, DeleteRange, Txn, Compact, the unary Lease calls) with it and passes the body along as `Request.Wire`. Puts keep `ParsePut`.
- **Entry.** `encodeBatch` appends `Request.Wire` as it is instead of marshaling the request again, so a transaction is encoded once, by its client. A LeaseGrant whose ID the node picks drops its wire form and is marshaled, since its request changed.
- **Apply.** Every write that is not a put is decoded with `UnmarshalAlias`, so the index keeps keys and values as slices of the entry on every replica.

Local: `go test -race -short` of server, core and node, 48 simulator seeds, the difftest against the recorded etcd v3.7.2 answers, and golangci-lint pass.

title: Fewer allocations per request on the batch path
body:
Part of #50. Stacked on #77; the base becomes `main` as #75, #76 and #77 merge.

The [benchmark on #75](https://github.com/djosh34/tigerstore/pull/75) measured 34.6 leader allocations per Put on #76 at 256 clients. This PR removes the per-request allocations that the batch path still has in the frontend and the core:

- **Header blocks.** x/net's `ReadMetaHeaders` built a `MetaHeadersFrame` with a fresh field slice for every request: 10 allocations per gRPC header block, measured with `testing.AllocsPerRun` on a grpc-go request. The reader now owns one `hpack.Decoder` whose emit function fills the request's fields directly. Once the fields are in the HPACK dynamic table, which happens from the second request on a connection, a block decodes with 0 allocations; `TestHeaderDecodeAllocs` holds that. The checks x/net made are kept: lowercase token field names, valid values, pseudo-fields first and only the known ones, and a 1 MiB limit on the decoded block. A block that breaks them resets its stream, and the HPACK state stays in step. CONTINUATION frames feed the same decoder; the Framer still checks their order.
- **Replies.** The Put replies of one completion batch are encoded into one shared buffer, each a clipped slice of it, instead of one buffer each.
- **Output items.** A stream's output slice starts with room for headers, message and trailers, so a unary reply no longer grows it twice.
- **Core bookkeeping.** `core.Node.SubmitAll` takes a batch's `pending` records in one allocation; the node driver uses it for `SubmitBatch`.

Tests: `go test -race -short` of server, node and core pass locally, 16 simulator seeds pass, and golangci-lint is clean. A Sol helper is benchmarking #77; this PR will get the same comparison.

title: Cold-restart check waits until the two nodes agree
body:
Part of #50, whose CI this blocked: `sim (3)` failed on #75 with seed 736998125, which fails the same way on main `e1fd889`.

```
seed 736998125: erasing node 3 at 17821 ms: the two restarted nodes did not converge: applied 112 and 111
```

Cause, traced with a throwaway print on main: in the cold restart, the leader (node 1, term 5) proposed a lease expiry as entry 112 at 5,998 ms of the 6 s window. It committed 112 at 5,999 ms and sent node 2 the new commit then. The window ended before node 2 received it. Its Raft progress showed node 2 in StateReplicate with match 112. So no entry was lost or stuck. The check stopped one message too early.

Fix:

- `coldRestart` runs on, a second at a time and at most 10 seconds, until both nodes have applied the same entries. The hash comparison after it is unchanged.
- `Sim.loop` used to pop the first event past `endAt` and drop it. It now leaves that event queued, so a run can resume. Runs that stop at their end behave as before; the dropped event was never traced.
- `TestColdRestartWaitsForLastCommit` runs seed 736998125. It fails on main and passes here.

Local: 64 seeds of `TestSeeds` passed.


Also in this PR: `TestSlowWatcherIsCut` (internal/node) failed on this PR's first CI run with "server stopped" on put 10. This PR does not touch that package. The test uses 10 ms ticks, so the leader's disk-stall watchdog (two election timeouts) fires after 200 ms of one fsync. My guess is a slow fsync on the shared runner; the test does not log why the node stopped, so the cause is not proven. The test now uses 50 ms ticks, a 1 s watchdog. It passes locally, and planted B13 is still caught.

title: Puts in wire form from the socket to the log, applied in place
body:
Part of #50. Stacked on #76 (and #75); the base becomes `main` as those merge.

The second step of the whole-batch write path: values stored once in the log and referenced by the index, and the batch encoded once and applied in place, from the [design change on #50](https://github.com/djosh34/tigerstore/issues/50) as corrected. This PR does it for Put, the request every benchmark measures. Txn, DeleteRange and the lease writes still decode at apply.

Put path after this PR:

1. The reader copies the request message out of the Framer once, into a buffer of its own size (as in #75).
2. `core.ParsePut` reads key, value, lease and flags in place with protowire. It follows protobuf's rules (the last value wins; unknown and mistyped fields are skipped), and `TestParsePutMatchesProtobuf` compares it with `proto.Unmarshal` on every truncation of tricky encodings.
3. `Submit` validates with `mvcc.CheckPutOp` and limits the size of the put as protobuf marshals it after a decode: the fields it holds plus unknown fields, as etcd does. A value field that a later one replaces does not count. `TestRequestSizeLimitMatchesEtcd` checks the wire form at etcd's boundary and a non-canonical put. `TestParsePutMatchesProtobuf` compares the size with `proto.Size` on every truncation. The difftest passed locally.
4. `Process` copies the client's bytes into the Raft entry. That is the one encode, into a buffer sized for the whole batch, so `append` never regrows it.
5. Every replica applies puts by walking the entry in place (`walkBatch`). The index keeps the key and value as slices of the entry. Previously each replica decoded a new `PutRequest` with fresh copies of key and value.
6. The reply is the revision, term and previous key (`core.Reply.Rev/Term/PrevKv`). The connection writer encodes the PutResponse by hand (`appendPutResponse`, compared byte for byte with protobuf in `TestPutResponseEncoding`), without building a response message.

Copies of a put value per node, counted from the code. The leader before this PR made a reader copy, the decode, the entry marshal and the apply decode, plus WAL and peer copies. After it, the reader copy and the entry copy remain, plus WAL and peer copies. Followers lose the apply decode copy.

The simulator now submits its puts in wire form, so it runs `ParsePut`, `checkPut` and the in-place apply. Its checks turn the reply back into a message with `core.Node.PutResponse`. The server's own PutResponse encoding is covered only by `TestPutResponseEncoding` and the server tests. 64 seeds of `TestSeeds` passed locally; CI runs the full campaigns and the planted bugs.

title: Whole-batch admission and grouped completion between connections and the committer
body:
Part of #50. Stacked on #75; the base becomes `main` once #75 merges.

The first step of the whole-batch write path from the [design change on #50](https://github.com/djosh34/tigerstore/issues/50): requests cross from a client connection to the committer, and replies come back, as batches instead of one at a time.

- **Admission.** The connection reader decodes every complete unary request the node runs (KV, Compact, and the unary Lease calls). It hands them to the node with one `Node.SubmitBatch` call when the next frame is not fully buffered yet, or at 256 requests or 4 MiB. There is no timer: a lone request goes out at once.
- **Completion.** After each `Process`, the committer groups the replies by connection and calls `Complete` once per connection with all of them. `Complete` only appends to the connection's queue and wakes its writer; the writer encodes the replies.
- **Gone from this path:** the goroutine, the context, the `request` struct and the reply channel per call, and the inbox send per call. A call the node runs now has no context of its own. The client enforces its `grpc-timeout`, the node's 7 s request timeout still applies, and a reset drops the reply.
- **Bounds.** A connection may have 64 MiB of request bytes unanswered by the node. Above that, its reader stops reading until replies come back. If the node stops, the writer fails every call the node still holds with "server stopped".
- `Node.Do` stays for `/health`, the keepalive stream and the rare calls (Status, MemberList).

Not in this PR: decoding values in wire form, encoding the entry once and applying it in place, and the allocation strategy experiment. Those are the next PRs.

Tests: the new `TestNodeStopsUnderLoad` stops a node while 50 calls wait on it, and every call must get an answer. The existing server tests and the #75 frontend tests pass with `-race`.

title: Custom HTTP/2 gRPC server on the client port
body:
Part of #50.

The client port now runs our own HTTP/2 gRPC server on x/net's Framer and HPACK, as the [design change on #50](https://github.com/djosh34/tigerstore/issues/50) decided. The `http.Server` + `grpc.Server.ServeHTTP` adapter from #65 is gone, and grpc-go's server is no longer used. This is the first piece. The whole-batch write path comes in the next PRs; here unary calls still run one goroutine and one `Node.Do` each.

What it serves:

- KV (Range, Put, DeleteRange, Txn, Compact), Lease (Grant, Revoke, TimeToLive, Leases, KeepAlive stream), Watch, Cluster.MemberList and Maintenance.Status. Other etcd methods, RangeStream included, answer Unimplemented with grpc-go's message.
- `GET /health` and `/version` on the same TLS port over HTTP/2, and over HTTP/1.1 for TLS clients that do not offer h2.
- The gaps the gRPC pre-work listed: `grpc-timeout` deadlines, `hasleader` on unary and streaming calls, GOAWAY on stop with a 1 s drain, a 4 MiB per-stream reply queue, a 20 s write deadline, client resets that cancel the call and drop late replies, receive and send flow control, and grpc-go's ResourceExhausted above the 2 MiB receive limit.

Layout: `server.go` accepts connections and does TLS. `h2.go` is the reader and connection state. `write.go` is the writer and send flow control. `stream.go` holds streams, message framing and the handler goroutines. `rpc.go` is the method table. `http.go` serves `/health` and `/version`.

Tests:

- New tests in `internal/server/h2_test.go`: HTTP/1.1 health and version, values near the request limit both ways (the reply exceeds the client's window), a request above the limit, deadline and require-leader without a quorum, Unimplemented methods, the keepalive stream, 200 calls canceled in flight, and a raw-frame client (settings, ping, a reset call with a late reply, RangeStream, GOAWAY on stop).
- The smoke job also runs etcdctl `lease grant/keep-alive --once/timetolive/revoke`, `compaction` and `member list`, and reads `/health` with `curl --http1.1`.
- Local runs: `go test -race -short ./internal/server/` passed, and `scripts/smoke.sh` passed with the local etcdctl 3.5.17. CI runs the smoke job with etcdctl 3.7.2.

A Sol helper will post benchmark numbers against main and etcd v3.7.2 here.

title: Suggestion from GPT Astra: reconsider whole-batch execution before micro-optimizing the current pipeline
body:
## Advisory suggestion from GPT Astra

The owner requested this report after a fresh GPT-6 Astra review at xhigh and a separate GPT-6.1 Sol source audit. This is a design suggestion, not a new requirement, acceptance gate, bug declaration, or instruction to stop the current work. It does not change #46 or any outcome's Done when. The architect may reject it and close this issue if the reasoning is wrong, the idea is not useful, or measurements favor the current design. Record a short reason if doing so.

Related work: #46, #47, #50, #52, the starting design in #32, and the owner directions in #53.

## Scope and evidence

Both auditors inspected main at `84c19cf5e76e67fa163c4be05de5c17250facd6d`. They used source files, pinned dependency source, and GitHub discussions. They did not run new builds, tests, benchmarks, or experiments. They did not contact the architect, workers, reviewers, or each other. No plan agent received this report as a message.

Main has advanced since that snapshot. At publication, GitHub reports `71f8b9dcb3670ef43d8b9f549140eb54cbda7236`. Findings below describe the audited snapshot, not a verification of that newer commit. Some findings may already be obsolete.

The reported 8,906 Put/s comes from the [PR #68 benchmark](https://github.com/djosh34/tigerstore/pull/68#issuecomment-6137442509), which measured candidate `b4fb26b`, not the exact audited snapshot. No new throughput result appears in this report.

## The owner's concern

The owner is concerned that the optimization phase may micro-optimize the current design instead of considering a radical, much faster execution design. The improvement loop had not happened at the time of this discussion, so the current implementation is acceptable as an intermediate step.

The main concern is whole-batch execution and memory ownership. Conceptually, allocate or reserve the small objects needed for a whole batch together, prepare them, execute the batch by walking those objects, and reclaim them together when the batch's users have finished. Packing individually allocated and individually admitted RPCs into one Raft entry is not the complete idea.

The owner also recognizes that this may not be the actual bottleneck. This report does not demand an arena allocator, custom queue, protocol rewrite, or any specific implementation. Those are experiments to judge by total CPU, memory, correctness and latency.

## Verdict

The implementers thought through the central single-owner design and produced real batching and scheduler evidence. They have not yet implemented the complete prepared, whole-batch execution pipeline described by the owner.

The measured configuration appears to exhaust its leader CPU at about 8.9k Put/s. That is a limit of the measured software and configuration, not a demonstrated limit of the intended architecture. There is no evidence that contention on an application-state mutex explains it.

## 1. Single ownership is real, but the pipeline is not lock-free

One committer goroutine owns RawNode, MVCC, revisions, leases, watches and request bookkeeping. RPC handlers do not mutate the store concurrently. The WAL worker owns disk execution. Peer writers own their connections.

Sources: [node driver](https://github.com/djosh34/tigerstore/blob/84c19cf5e76e67fa163c4be05de5c17250facd6d/internal/node/node.go#L228-L340) and [core state](https://github.com/djosh34/tigerstore/blob/84c19cf5e76e67fa163c4be05de5c17250facd6d/internal/core/node.go#L136-L173).

The implementation still executes synchronization:

| Mechanism | Actual use |
| --- | --- |
| Tigerstore state mutex | No tigerstore-authored mutex protects application state. |
| Raft storage mutex | `core.storage` embeds `raft.MemoryStorage`. Its Append, SetHardState, Entries, Term and related methods take a mutex. |
| B-tree mutex | The Google B-tree's node freelist locks its allocation and free paths. Ordinary existing-key lookup does not take that freelist lock. |
| Channels | RPC admission and replies, disk jobs and completions, peer queues and watch responses use Go channels. Channels use runtime locks. |
| Atomics | Request IDs, published leader ID and peer queue-byte accounting use atomics. |
| Peer registry mutex | A mutex protects connection tracking and shutdown, not ordinary state application or message enqueue. |
| Transport/runtime synchronization | HTTP/2, gRPC, TLS and runtime scheduling add their own synchronization. |

Sources: [storage wrapper](https://github.com/djosh34/tigerstore/blob/84c19cf5e76e67fa163c4be05de5c17250facd6d/internal/core/storage.go#L13-L45), [Raft v3.7.0 MemoryStorage](https://github.com/etcd-io/raft/blob/v3.7.0/storage.go#L104-L199), [B-tree v1.1.3 freelist](https://github.com/google/btree/blob/v1.1.3/btree_generic.go#L85-L120), [Go channel implementation](https://github.com/golang/go/blob/go1.27.2/src/runtime/chan.go#L34-L55), and [peer transport](https://github.com/djosh34/tigerstore/blob/84c19cf5e76e67fa163c4be05de5c17250facd6d/internal/peer/peer.go#L73-L174).

The storage and index dependency locks should be uncontended under single ownership. Their existence does not prove they cost meaningful throughput. Removing every mutex is not the suggested first experiment.

The accurate description is one application-state owner with asynchronous adapters. It is one owning goroutine, not a permanently bound OS thread or a single-threaded process.

## 2. Batching happens inside Raft and disk, but requests still cross individually

The audited write path does the following:

1. HTTP/2 and gRPC handle each request and decode its protobuf outside the owner.
2. `Node.Do` allocates a request and buffered reply channel, increments an atomic ID and sends one inbox event per RPC.
3. The owner drains individual events. Each request calls Submit, which validates, sizes and classifies it and creates pending bookkeeping.
4. The owner protobuf-encodes each request into a packed Raft entry.
5. Peer writers and the WAL worker replicate and persist that entry asynchronously.
6. Every replica decodes each committed command again on its owner, executes it and constructs response objects.
7. The originating node completes each request through its individual reply channel.
8. gRPC serializes the response after committed execution.

Sources: [per-request admission and driver drain](https://github.com/djosh34/tigerstore/blob/84c19cf5e76e67fa163c4be05de5c17250facd6d/internal/node/node.go#L206-L298), [validation and proposal](https://github.com/djosh34/tigerstore/blob/84c19cf5e76e67fa163c4be05de5c17250facd6d/internal/core/node.go#L306-L480), [batch codec](https://github.com/djosh34/tigerstore/blob/84c19cf5e76e67fa163c4be05de5c17250facd6d/internal/core/codec.go#L34-L125), and [committed application](https://github.com/djosh34/tigerstore/blob/84c19cf5e76e67fa163c4be05de5c17250facd6d/internal/core/node.go#L697-L753).

Draining 4,096 inputs amortizes a Process call. It does not amortize their earlier inbox sends, per-request channels and allocations, blocked handlers, or later completion notifications. Packing requests amortizes Raft bookkeeping, but generated protobuf decode and response construction remain per operation.

This is the strongest mismatch with the owner's whole-batch concept.

A possible experiment would give helpers immutable command descriptors backed by batch-owned memory, admit descriptors as batches, walk them on the owner, and hand completion batches to connection writers. This can retain unary etcd RPC semantics and avoid a fill timer. It does not require changing the public client API.

Batch-wide reclamation needs explicit lifetimes. Raft, the WAL worker, peer writers, retries, MVCC values and slow clients may retain different parts of a batch. A single free cannot happen while any of them still references it. A stalled client must not pin unlimited batch memory. Slabs, separate payload lifetimes or bounded pins may fit better than one literal allocation and free. The experiment should count allocations, retained bytes, wakeups and CPU per operation rather than assume an allocator change will help.

## 3. The batching and scheduler work is substantive

The leader holds local proposals until the append carrying its preceding local batch is durable. Forwarded proposals and hard-state-only appends do not extend that hold. A byte cap can send a full entry early. Ready processing continues. Leadership changes reset the hold. The disk worker drains ordered jobs and syncs them as one group.

The PR reviews found and corrected forwarded-write starvation and zero-payload accounting. The [batch tests](https://github.com/djosh34/tigerstore/blob/84c19cf5e76e67fa163c4be05de5c17250facd6d/internal/core/batch_test.go) cover those cases.

The [batch256 investigation](https://github.com/djosh34/tigerstore/issues/47#issuecomment-6137116710) found that one Go execution processor could stop intake during blocking fsync. Same-binary processor-count changes and a syscall-handoff control supported that explanation. The command now enforces at least two Go processors, even with one physical CPU assigned to a node.

Two Go processors do not violate single ownership and do not provide two physical cores. Helpers, TLS, the owner and GC still share the assigned CPU. The benefit is progress while one goroutine blocks in a syscall.

The batching model still has conditions. Groups contain requests that reach admission, not all offered arrivals. Follower proposals enter the leader through Step rather than its local accumulator. The peer window has both a 32 MiB byte cap and a 256-message cap. Closed-loop response scheduling, entry sizes and CPU cost affect batch growth. The formula `batch size = arrival rate × append time` is a useful approximation, not a demonstrated steady-state guarantee.

## 4. Why HTTP and gRPC exist

Client-facing etcd v3 compatibility requires gRPC over HTTP/2. Stock kube-apiserver and etcd clients must still work. A custom client-facing implementation can speak the same wire protocol, but replacing it with an incompatible private protocol would change an owner-fixed requirement.

Peer traffic already uses a private transport: length-prefixed Raft messages over TLS/TCP. It does not use peer gRPC. The architect explicitly permitted Raft's protobuf message encoding in the [transport clarification](https://github.com/djosh34/tigerstore/issues/47#issuecomment-6133969290). A custom peer codec remains an experiment.

The current TLS client listener uses `http.Server` and routes gRPC to `grpc.Server.ServeHTTP`. That lets `/health` and `/version` share the client port. It is a choice of implementation, not a requirement that the fast path use ServeHTTP.

The earlier prototype's base used grpc-go's native TLS transport. The [transport experiment](https://github.com/djosh34/tigerstore/issues/47#issuecomment-6134109817) also found substantial differences between frontend implementations. A matched comparison of native grpc-go and ServeHTTP is worth considering before a full protocol rewrite. Neither auditor proved this explains the durable throughput gap.

Sources: [current server](https://github.com/djosh34/tigerstore/blob/84c19cf5e76e67fa163c4be05de5c17250facd6d/internal/server/server.go#L58-L99), [HTTP routing](https://github.com/djosh34/tigerstore/blob/84c19cf5e76e67fa163c4be05de5c17250facd6d/internal/server/http.go#L23-L33), and [older native gRPC server](https://github.com/djosh34/tigerstore/blob/b8bac8b371c94f6d17136ad14aaa04354bbff01e/internal/server/server.go#L44-L57).

## 5. Precommit responses need a complete ordering design

The [design document](https://github.com/djosh34/tigerstore/blob/84c19cf5e76e67fa163c4be05de5c17250facd6d/docs/design.md) explicitly says responses are not prepared before commit yet. Its suggestion to run application ahead on a copy does not fully specify the protocol.

A response-plan experiment would need to handle:

- The actual ordered log prefix, including forwarded commands, inherited entries, lease mutations and compaction.
- CAS results, transaction branches and revisions derived from execution outcomes. A failed CAS or no-op does not necessarily consume a revision.
- Separate committed visibility and speculative state. Reads and watches must not observe speculation.
- Plans bound to term, log index, command position and origin request identity.
- Endpoint-specific headers and local watch registrations. A leader-prepared body is not automatically a complete follower-origin reply.
- Late encoder completions and leadership or suffix changes. Discard stale derived plans without assuming the underlying command can never commit.
- Commit arriving before encoding. The owner must not block on a helper.
- Avoiding duplicate full execution unless the measured latency gain justifies the added CPU and memory.

Helpers can parse, structurally validate, size, encode and work on immutable owner-approved data. They cannot independently choose CAS outcomes, revisions or lease validity from mutable live state.

On one saturated physical CPU, moving work to another goroutine does not remove that work. Speculative execution plus repeated committed execution may hurt throughput. Measure it.

## 6. Asynchronous disk work does not bound owner CPU work

Large operations still run synchronously on the owner:

- Range walks matching keys to compute Count even when the returned values have a limit.
- Compaction walks all keys and edits version slices.
- Historical watch creation gathers and sorts history and constructs catch-up responses before returning.
- Live matching walks watchers and changes.
- Lease revocation sorts and deletes all attached keys.

Sources: [Range](https://github.com/djosh34/tigerstore/blob/84c19cf5e76e67fa163c4be05de5c17250facd6d/internal/mvcc/ops.go#L67-L105), [history and compaction](https://github.com/djosh34/tigerstore/blob/84c19cf5e76e67fa163c4be05de5c17250facd6d/internal/mvcc/store.go#L199-L263), and [watch processing](https://github.com/djosh34/tigerstore/blob/84c19cf5e76e67fa163c4be05de5c17250facd6d/internal/core/watch.go#L198-L285).

A response-size limit is not a core-turn time budget. These operations can delay unrelated requests and control processing with no contended state mutex.

Bounded continuations, pinned read revisions, current-count indexes and ordered history access are possible experiments. Atomic transactions must remain atomic. Yielding to control work must not expose half of a delete or revoke.

Values also remain in both retained log entries and decoded MVCC storage. The full log grows in memory and on disk until checkpoints and cleaning exist. Eliminating duplicate value copies helps memory but does not solve retention by itself.

## 7. Backpressure does not yet guarantee control progress

The transport has separate outbound control and data queues, byte estimates and write deadlines. Persistence completions have a separate channel. Those are useful mechanisms.

The driver still uses an 8,192-event shared inbox, count-bounded persistence queues and a 4,096-response watch queue. These do not form an aggregate byte budget. Near-limit writes alone could retain about 12 GiB of payload in a full inbox, before other memory.

When the persistence backlog reaches its limit, the driver disables the shared inbox. That stops incoming peer messages as well as client admission. Deliver blocks when that inbox is full, so the receiver cannot read later frames on that connection. Outbound priority cannot bypass a frame already being written or bytes already queued in TCP.

Sources: [admission and backlog](https://github.com/djosh34/tigerstore/blob/84c19cf5e76e67fa163c4be05de5c17250facd6d/internal/node/node.go#L166-L283) and [peer receive and send](https://github.com/djosh34/tigerstore/blob/84c19cf5e76e67fa163c4be05de5c17250facd6d/internal/peer/peer.go#L219-L318).

The proposal gate keeps control work moving while it waits. That does not prove end-to-end control progress under overload. A whole-batch design should measure retained bytes, maximum owner-turn duration and healthy-majority progress under stalled disks, peers and clients.

## 8. What the performance evidence establishes

The [PR #68 report](https://github.com/djosh34/tigerstore/pull/68#issuecomment-6137442509) measured the following medians:

| Clients | Put/s | Leader CPU microseconds/Put | Leader Puts/file-fsync |
| ---: | ---: | ---: | ---: |
| 64 | 8,906 | 109.833 | 16.138 |
| 256 | 7,950 | 125.167 | 11.570 |

Rate multiplied by leader CPU per operation is approximately one CPU-second per second. These are independent medians, so this is a consistency check, not a newly measured occupancy result. It suggests the measured leader process has little unused CPU.

That CPU belongs to the entire process, not just ordered state-machine execution. It includes transport, allocation, runtime and other work. No current attribution proves which part dominates.

The older two-processor prototype reached about 29.7k Put/s under different source and configuration. It does not certify the current implementation or promise its achievable speed. The old 90k forecast is also a hypothesis.

The published comparison used free ARM runners, one physical CPU per replica and one for the generator, TLS, disk barriers, and five repetitions with candidate, main and etcd 3.7.2 back to back in each concurrency job. It used leader-only closed-loop 1 KiB Puts over 4,096 keys. It did not exercise regional delay, mixed follower ingress, CAS mixtures, watches or compaction. Candidate servers used two Go processors while main and etcd used one. Source ancestry and scheduler changes prevent a batching-only attribution. Physical disk groups and logical entry batches are different measurements.

No new benchmark ran for this issue.

## 9. Suggested experiments for the improvement loop

These are options, not a required checklist. The architect can change their order, replace them or reject them.

1. Explain the current leader CPU cost on one exact source. Compare native grpc-go with ServeHTTP and isolate the proposal gate and Go-processor policy. Give etcd the same physical layout and scheduler opportunity. Measure owner CPU separately from total process CPU, allocation bytes, wakeups, operations per entry, entries per fsync and append-to-next-proposal delay. Keep intrusive traces out of headline runs.
2. Try a whole-batch allocation, preparation, admission, execution and completion path. Compare it with individual Node.Do calls. Test immutable command representations and wire-backed values separately. Include delayed reclamation, cancellation, retries, stale completions and slow clients. Retain only changes with measured gains.
3. Compare leader-only and balanced follower ingress with a lean generator, then regional delay. Report open-loop latency and queue growth as well as closed-loop capacity. Determine whether tiny forwarded entries undo local batching benefits.
4. Test owner work at useful object counts with Range, watch catch-up, compaction, writes and stalled peers or disks. Measure turn duration, retained bytes and control progress. Preserve transaction atomicity and watch continuity.
5. Prototype response plans with dependent CAS, failed-branch reads, leases, forwarded requests and leadership replacement. Compare planned outcomes with ordinary committed application, then measure CPU, memory and commit-to-reply latency. Do not integrate speculation just because it sounds faster.

All experiments keep the owner-fixed guarantees. Async Raft persistence responses must retain their ordered dependencies. No early publication, no acknowledgement before the required durable application, and no weakening of acknowledged-value survival across node loss.

## Closing recommendation

Keep whole-design candidates in the tournament. Do not let the existing per-RPC Node.Do interface define the limits of every optimization idea. A candidate may replace the frontend adapter, admission/completion model, command representation, batch memory ownership or state-machine execution arrangement while preserving the public API and guarantees.

The current implementation is a useful correctness base. Its benchmark is not proof that the intended batched runner has reached its limit. The concern is premature commitment to this implementation, not a demand to rewrite it before the improvement loop.

This issue can be closed if the architect judges it unhelpful or evidence favors the current design. It is advisory, not a merge blocker or a new outcome requirement.

title: Planted bugs B05, B13, B14 and B16
body:
Part of #47.

Stacked on #72. This adds the last four planted bugs of the #47 inventory. The owner's decision on #47 says a bug that targets code this design lacks is replaced by the nearest real bug of the same class.

- **B05 (snapshot authority before sync) → a new WAL segment takes records before its directory entry is synced.** There are no snapshots. This is the same class: new on-disk state used before its metadata is durable. The simulator catches it at seed 1: an erase-one-disk cold restart loses applied entries.
- **B16 (unlink before replacement sync) → WAL rotation moves to a new segment without the old one's last sync.** There is no segment cleaning. Same class: old data left behind before it is durable. Caught at seed 1.
- **B13 (slow watcher blocks apply):** the node driver blocks on a full watch queue instead of closing the stream. `internal/node` gets its first test, `TestSlowWatcherIsCut`. It runs one node with a queue of 8 responses (new `node.Config.WatchQueue`) and a stream that is never read, then makes 50 writes. The stream must close with `ErrWatchTooSlow`, and a Put and a Range must each finish within 10 election timeouts. With the bug on, put 9 times out.
- **B14 (peer writer without a write deadline):** the writer gets no deadline. `TestStalledPeerIsDropped` in `internal/peer` puts a TCP proxy between two transports. The proxy stops reading one connection while 25 MiB is queued behind it. The 5 s write deadline must drop that connection, and a message sent after the stall must arrive over a new one. title: Gray nodes and clients, crashes inside recovery, and a commit watchdog
body:
Part of #47.

Stacked on #71. This covers the remaining fault families from #47's Done when and #33: gray nodes, gray clients, and crashes during WAL recovery, each with a numeric bound.

- **Commit watchdog (core).** A leader stops with `ErrCommitStalled` when its own entries have waited three election timeouts to commit. A gray leader whose heartbeats get through but whose appends do not passes Raft's quorum check while nothing commits; this is #33's gray-leader trap. Three is above the disk watchdog's two, so a stalled disk is caught first.
- **Gray nodes (sim).** About every 8 s, and once in every run, a gray period of 2 to 6 s starts. One node at a time is gray, and the gray node may change every 1 to 3 s. Heartbeats, votes and responses to and from it pass; appends do not. In half the cases its fsyncs also take 0.5 to 3 s.
- **Gray client (sim).** It opens a stream with 10 watches (a quarter from revision 1), never reads it, and reconnects every 50 to 300 ms until healing. `checkWatchersFreed` then requires that nodes hold only the watchers of open streams.
- **Crashes inside recovery (sim).** One restart in three during the faults crashes again at its first to fourth writing disk operation inside `wal.Open`, then starts over from what the disk holds.
- **Tests.**
  - `TestGrayLeaderIsReplaced`: the gray leader stops within 3 election timeouts plus 2 ticks, and calls to the other two nodes succeed in under a second from 3 election timeouts after that.
  - `TestEachFaultTakesEffect` now covers gray nodes, the gray client and recovery crashes.
  - `TestSeeds` requires a gray node and gray-client streams in every run, and a stopped gray leader and a recovery crash over 64+ seeds.

Not covered: a slowed CPU (each core step costing virtual time). Snapshot install does not exist yet, so the simulator cannot crash inside it.

Local: 16 seeds, `TestLinearizable` on 16 seeds, the gray-leader, stalled-leader and half-open tests, and every `TestEachFaultTakesEffect` case pass under the #46 memory rule.
