title: Network, pause and clock faults in the simulator; all 64 link masks
body:
Part of #47

Second piece of the simulator's full fault set: network, pauses and clocks. Stacked on #69 (base `work/47-diskfaults`).

- **All 64 directed-link masks:** `TestAllLinkMasks` holds each of the 64 sets of directed links between the three nodes for 3 s (from 2 s), with no other fault, then heals. Every rule of the simulator and every checker of #56 must hold, Porcupine included (4 clients, no leases), and the cluster must serve 2 s after healing. It runs in about 5 s.
- **Switching:** `TestSwitchingLinks` switches to a random mask about every 300 ms for 10 s, 3 seeds.
- **Asymmetric and switching delays:** every link change draws a new delay profile per directed link (base 20 µs to 2 ms, jitter up to the base), so the two directions of a pair differ and delays switch over time; the occasional long delay up to `MaxDelay` stays.
- **Link stalls (head-of-line blocking):** about every 4 s one directed link holds everything for 0.5 to 2 s, then delivers in order.
- **Process pauses:** about every 6 s a node handles nothing for 0.2 to 2 s, then everything at once and in order (ticks, messages, disk completions, requests).
- **Clock skew and jumps:** each node ticks up to 5% fast or slow, and about every 6 s a node's clock jumps forward by up to 3 ticks, at most once per node in 10 s. This is the declared clock envelope; the lease lower bound allows 5% of the TTL plus one 3-tick jump.
- **Liveness:** calls to a paused node are exempt, like calls to a stalled disk.
- Bug fixed on the way: `setLinks` walked the nodes, so links set before the nodes existed stayed down; it walks the links now.

Evidence on 85e54a7, small local runs: 4 seeds of `TestSeeds`, `TestLinearizable` and `TestStalledLeaderIsReplaced` pass (2 to 3 pauses per seed); `TestAllLinkMasks` (64 masks) and `TestSwitchingLinks` pass; `golangci-lint` 0 issues. CI runs the 1,600 seeds with all faults on.

Still to come in #47: gray clients and the planted-bug inventory with its CI gate.

title: Disk faults in the simulator, a stalled leader fences itself, erase-one-disk
body:
Part of #47

First piece of the simulator's full fault set: disk faults and erase-one-disk. Stacked on #68 (base `work/47-batch`).

- **Failing writes and syncs:** about every 6 virtual seconds the next write or sync of a node fails with EIO, or a write is short with ENOSPC. The node stops at once, never retries the fsync, and restarts from its disk (simfs crash semantics, so unsynced bytes go). One such fault per run is guaranteed.
- **Stalls:** about every 8 s a node's disk stalls for 1.5 to 4 s.
- **Stalled leader fences itself (core):** a leader whose own append has been on its way to disk for 2 election timeouts stops with `ErrDiskStalled`. A stalled leader still heartbeats, so nobody replaces it, and its own clients hang. The followers still commit without it, since their two acks are a quorum. `TestStalledLeaderIsReplaced` stalls the leader for good with no other fault and requires that it stops and that every call to a healthy node 10 election timeouts later succeeds. With the watchdog disabled, the test fails.
- **Detectable damage:** at one crash in five (until once per run), the crashed node's synced bytes are damaged away from the newest tail, like a misdirected write. The node must refuse to start with `wal.ErrCorrupt` and stays fenced for the rest of the run. Starting on a damaged disk fails the run. Lost writes are a lying disk, outside the guarantee.
- **Erase-one-disk:** at a checkpoint in the faulty phase and at the end, each node's disk is erased in turn. The other two cold-start alone from copies of their synced bytes (a pair with a damaged disk is skipped) and must hold every write acknowledged before the checkpoint.
- **Liveness rule:** calls to a fenced node (a real client moves on) and to a node with a stalled disk (it cannot apply) are exempt. Healing clears armed disk faults.
- `docs/design.md` describes all of it.

Evidence on 2d4843a, small local runs (memory rule on #46):
- 4 seeds of `TestSeeds` and `TestLinearizable`: 1 to 7 disk faults, 0 to 1 stalled-leader stops, 0 to 1 fenced nodes and 2 to 6 cold restarts per seed. `TestStalledLeaderIsReplaced` passes 3 seeds.
- Planted: an fsync EIO treated as success fails seed 1 (raft panics on a lost log tail, "tocommit(483) is out of range [lastIndex(482)]"). A disabled watchdog fails `TestStalledLeaderIsReplaced`.
- `go test` for core, simfs, wal; `golangci-lint` 0 issues.

Next pieces: network faults (all 64 masks, switching, asymmetric delays, stalls, half-open), pauses and clock skew, then the planted-bug inventory with its CI gate.

title: Self-clocked write batching in the core
body:
Part of #47

The write batching that #47's Done when and `docs/design.md` require. Stacked on #67 (base `work/47-lease`; retargeted before #67 merges).

**Problem.** The [profiling pre-work on #50](https://github.com/djosh34/tigerstore/issues/50#issuecomment-6134975020) found the leader at 1.8 Puts per fsync at 256 clients, spending about 77% of wall time in fsync: each core turn proposed what arrived since the last turn, usually one write.

**Change, in the core, not the driver.** While the leader has a local append with entries on its way to disk, `Process` holds new writes. When that append is `Persisted`, the next `Process` sends all held writes as one entry. The 4 MiB byte cap still sends a full entry early. Unlike the [group-commit pre-work](https://github.com/djosh34/tigerstore/issues/47)'s prototype, nothing else is gated:
- hard-state-only appends (a moved commit index) hold nothing, so one client never waits an extra fsync;
- followers forward proposals at once;
- `Ready` keeps running, so heartbeats, votes, ReadIndex, replies, timeouts and watch events never wait for the disk.
The driver already writes all queued append jobs with one write and one fsync. No timer.

**Tests.** `TestWritesWaitForTheLeadersAppend` holds one append, submits 50 writes one at a time with a `Process` after each, checks nothing goes out, releases the append and gets exactly one entry of 50 writes, then all 51 replies. The simulator runs the new path on every seed (3 seeds passed locally; CI runs 1,600). `go test` for core and server pass; `golangci-lint` 0 issues.

**Measurement:** a Sol helper reruns the group-commit pre-work's benchmark (free ARM runner, 16/64/256 clients, five repetitions, etcd 3.7.2 in the same job) with main and this branch, and posts the numbers here. Until then this PR claims fewer fsyncs per write by construction, not a measured speedup.

title: Leases: grant, revoke, keepalive, expiry, TimeToLive and Leases
body:
Part of #47

Leases, stacked on #66 (base `work/47-compact`; retargeted before #66 merges).

- **core.State:** the replicated state is now the index plus the leases, and `State.Apply` runs one committed write against both. The node and the simulator's model use it.
- **Rules, from etcd v3.7.2 and the semantics pre-work on #47:** a grant with ID 0 gets an ID before proposal (positive, per node and boot); TTL below 2 s becomes 2 s, above 9e9 s is `too large lease TTL`; a taken ID is `lease already exists`; negative IDs work; grants keep the revision. Keys move between leases on every write (put without lease and delete detach, `ignore_lease` keeps). Revoke deletes the keys in one transaction, so they share one revision; an empty lease moves no revision; a missing lease, 0 included, is NotFound.
- **Expiry:** only the leader keeps expiry, in ticks; it proposes the revoke of an expired lease and retries every 10 ticks. A new leader gives every lease its full TTL, as etcd's promotion does.
- **Keepalive** is a Raft entry that renews on the leader when it applies; a missing lease gets TTL 0. **TimeToLive** (leader's remaining seconds, granted TTL elsewhere, -1 when missing) and **Leases** are linearizable reads. The gRPC Lease service serves all five.
- **Bug found and fixed:** watchers matched the index's change list after every write. A grant or keepalive changes no key, so they re-sent the previous write's events. `State.Changes` is now empty for such writes.
- **difftest:** the lease cases leave the expected-failure list, which is now empty: every recorded step matches etcd v3.7.2 (or its stricter answer).
- **sim:** clients grant 2 to 4 s leases, put keys with their newest lease, keep it alive and revoke. The model replays the log through `core.State`. At the end, every lease still granted must have been granted or kept alive within 8 s, so expiry is checked. The history gets an ambiguous expiry op per granted lease (#56's way of modelling expiry) and leaves keepalives out. Porcupine's short runs leave leases out: with them, two of three runs timed out after a minute. The full runs keep leases for the other checkers.

Evidence on a8d5dc5, run small because of the shared host's memory (new rule on #46):
- `TestLeaseRules`, `TestLeaseExpiry` (two keys expire at one revision, a keepalive pushes expiry back), `go test` for core, mvcc, server; `golangci-lint` (0 issues); `scripts/difftest.sh tigerstore` passes with no expected failures.
- 3 seeds of `TestSeeds` (107 to 144 revokes each) and `TestLinearizable` pass; CI runs the 1,600 seeds.
- Planted, 3 seeds each: a leader that never expires leases fails seed 1 ("lease ... was last granted or kept alive at 12345 ms but still lives at 33000 ms"); a put without a lease that keeps the key attached fails #56's durability checker; a revoke that takes a revision per key fails seed 3's watch check.

title: Compact: MVCC compaction through Raft, watch cancels, simulated compactions
body:
Part of #47

Compact, stacked on #65 (base `work/47-api`; I retarget to main before #65 merges).

- **mvcc:** `Store.Compact(C)` follows etcd v3.7.2 and the semantics pre-work on #47. C at or below the last compaction is `ErrCompacted` (so are 0 and -1 after one), above the current revision is `ErrFutureRev`, and the revision does not change. Per key it keeps the newest version at or below C and everything after; a tombstone before C goes, with the key if nothing remains; a tombstone at C stays so a watch from C still gets that delete. Reads at C work, below C fail.
- **core:** Compact is a Raft entry kind (physical is the same, since compaction happens at once). A watch from below C gets etcd's answer: created, then canceled with `compact_revision` C, empty reason, header revision 0. A watch with `prev_kv` from C itself is canceled the same way, because its first events would lack previous values; the difftest's stricter list allows exactly this answer and not etcd's.
- **server:** `KV.Compact`.
- **difftest:** the compaction cases leave the expected-failure list and match etcd (or the stricter answer).
- **sim:** clients compact about once in 100 calls, a little behind the newest revision they saw. Checks now use a model: the committed log replayed without compactions, which must end in the cluster's state. A watch canceled by compaction ends that logical watch and starts a new one from now; each logical watch must match the history. Liveness after healing accepts definite answers such as "compacted". Each seed must have at least one successful compaction.

Evidence on fb73af5:
- `scripts/difftest.sh tigerstore` passes.
- 8 seeds: 41 to 68 successful compactions and 8 to 17 compaction-canceled watches each; 200 fresh seeds (20000 to 20199) pass `TestSeeds` and `TestLinearizable` with #56's checkers.
- Planted: compaction that also drops the version at C fails seed 1 ("replaying the committed log gives revision 2409 ..., the cluster has revision 2474"). Not canceling a prev_kv watch from C passes 8 sim seeds (a resume landing exactly on C is rare there) but fails three difftest steps and `TestWatchFromCompactedRevision`.
- `TestCompact`, `TestWatchFromCompactedRevision`, `go test -short ./...`, `golangci-lint` (0 issues).

Not in this PR: segment cleaning. MVCC compaction frees index versions, but the Raft log still keeps every entry, so the log and memory only grow; the design doc says so under Seams.

title: Maintenance.Status, /health and /version, etcd's request size limit
body:
Part of #47

The small API pieces of #47's Done when, and bug #62.

- **#62, request size:** etcd v3.7.2 limits the size of the marshaled `InternalRaftRequest` that wraps a write, including a header with a request ID. The core now sizes writes the same way with a 10-byte varint ID (etcd's IDs from the difftest member have the top bit set). The largest accepted value for a 39-byte key is now 1,572,801 for Put and 1,572,793 for a Txn put, etcd's numbers. Reads do not go through Raft in etcd and have only gRPC's limit here too. `TestRequestSizeLimitMatchesEtcd`, and the `max-request-size` difftest case leaves the expected-failure list.
- **Maintenance.Status:** version 3.7.2, storage version 3.7.0, leader, term, commit index, applied index, 2 GiB quota, "etcdserver: no leader" in Errors without a leader, and the estimated log size as database size (never 0, since etcdctl's table divides by it). Facts from the semantics pre-work on #47.
- **GET /health and /version on the client port:** with TLS, the port is an `http.Server` over HTTP/2 that sends `application/grpc` requests to `grpc.Server.ServeHTTP`, as etcd does. The bodies and status codes match the pre-work's captured etcd 3.7.2 responses: `{"etcdserver":"3.7.2","etcdcluster":"3.7.0","storage":"3.7.0"}`; `{"health":"true","reason":""}`; 503 `{"health":"false","reason":"RAFT NO LEADER"}\n` via `http.Error`; `?serializable=true` skips the leader check.
- **RangeStream:** stays `Unimplemented` (Kubernetes 1.37 falls back on that code); now tested.
- **smoke:** etcdctl endpoint status (table and JSON), curl `/version` and `/health`.

Tests on 7052e6e: `TestStatusHealthVersionRangeStream` (Status fields, RangeStream code, exact /version and /health bodies, /health 503 after two of three nodes stop), `go test -race` for `server`, `go test -short ./...`, `golangci-lint` (0 issues), `scripts/smoke.sh`, and `scripts/difftest.sh tigerstore` pass locally.

Leases and Compact come next, each in its own PR.

title: Faster set comparison in the Porcupine model
body:
Part of #47.

Fixes the `sim (2)` failure on PR #63's commit `bcf40d5`. There, `TestLinearizable/660415350` timed out: "linearizability check of 1545 operations timed out after 1m0s". The seed is drawn from the run ID, so any PR can hit it. That PR does not touch the checker or the simulator.

Locally on this host (8 ARM64 cores, Go 1.27.2) the same seed took 40.5 s before this change. A CPU profile put 71% of the time in Porcupine's cache lookup (`cacheContains`). The lookup compares sets of model states, and each comparison checked every pair of states field by field.

The change:
- Each model state keeps an FNV-1a fingerprint of its revisions, leases and key fields, with values counted by length only.
- A set of states is sorted by fingerprint. Two sets compare by length, then by fingerprints, and only then state by state.
- Equal fingerprints are always confirmed with a full comparison, so the result does not change.

After the change the same seed takes 14.9 s. Every other seed of that CI shard (660415144 to 660415543) finished in milliseconds before and after. 1,545 versus 1,634 operations is not a determinism problem: the checker counts after dropping reads that failed ambiguously, and the test counts all calls.

`TestStatesEqual` covers the set comparison. A probe that trusted fingerprints alone failed it with "sets that differ only in a value of the same length compare equal".

Porcupine's own search (`bitset.equals`, 21%) and GC are what is left. A seed whose history branches more can still time out, and that stays a failure. Making the simulator's Porcupine runs smaller is the simulator's call.

title: Differential tests against etcd v3.7.2
body:
Part of #47.

Sequential differential tests against etcd v3.7.2 for the boundaries in `docs/design.md`: compaction at R-1, R and R+1, error codes and the maximum request size. Also the request shapes kube-apiserver sends, and leases. The tests run against both etcd and tigerstore.

## How it works

- `difftest/` sends requests over the raw etcd v3 gRPC API, so codes and messages are compared exactly as they arrive. Revisions are recorded relative to the start of each case, and lease IDs by the order the case granted them. A case's answers therefore do not depend on what ran before. Watches record everything that arrives within one second.
- Watches also record the created and cancel headers. They check that every other response keeps the created watch ID and has a header revision that does not go back and covers its events. Txn put and delete results record their header revision. A grant with an explicit ID records whether it got that ID.
- `difftest/testdata/etcd-v3.7.2.json` holds etcd v3.7.2's answers. `scripts/difftest.sh etcd record` writes it from a fresh single-node etcd on fixed ports. Two recordings in a row gave byte-identical files.
- `scripts/difftest.sh etcd|tigerstore` starts a fresh server and runs the tests. For tigerstore that is a 3-node TLS cluster built from the checkout, through `scripts/local-cluster.sh`. The script fails if a port is already in use, or if a server it started exited during the tests, so it never tests a leftover server.
- CI gets a `difftest` job for each server. It downloads etcd v3.7.2, checks its SHA-256, and runs the script. `ci` now needs it. golangci-lint now builds with the `difftest` tag.

## Where tigerstore may differ

The strict watch rule (`stricter` in `boundaries_test.go`): after a compaction at C, etcd v3.7.2 sends the update at C without `prev_kv`, because the version before C is compacted. Kubernetes rejects that event. For these three steps tigerstore must send the previous value or cancel the watch as compacted at C. etcd's answer is accepted only when the server is etcd:

- `compact-below-current`: watch a from 2 with prev_kv
- `compact-physical`: watch a from 2 with prev_kv
- `compact-at-current`: watch a from 3 with prev_kv

Expected failures (`expectedFail`). These run on every PR. `difftest/testdata/tigerstore-known.json` holds tigerstore's current answer to each listed step, and a listed step must give exactly that answer. `scripts/difftest.sh tigerstore record` writes that file again. A listed step that starts to match etcd fails the test, so the list must shrink as the core grows. On main `b8bac8b`:

- **Compaction, not built yet (#47):**
  - `compact-below-current`: compact at R-1, range a at 1, watch a from 1 with prev_kv, compact at R-1 again, compact at R-2
  - `compact-at-current`: compact at R, range a at 1, range a at 2, watch a from 1 and from 2 with prev_kv, compact at R again
  - `compact-above-current`: compact at R+1
  - `compact-physical`: physical compact at R-1, range a at 1, watch a from 1 with prev_kv
  - `error-codes`: compact at 2, txn with a historical range at a compacted revision, compact at revision 0, compact at revision -1
- **Leases, not built yet (#47):** all 17 steps of `leases`.
- **Request size limit, #62:** `max-request-size`, the largest put and the largest txn put. For a 39-byte key, tigerstore accepts 1,572,819 and 1,572,811 bytes, while etcd accepts 1,572,801 and 1,572,793. The core checks the client request's size. etcd checks its internal Raft request, which is larger. The steps one byte below, at and one byte above each limit match etcd.

Every other step matches etcd v3.7.2 on tigerstore. That covers the Kubernetes create, update and delete txns, failed CAS with the failure-branch range, the compactor's VERSION txn, limited, counted and keys-only lists at a revision, watches with and without prev_kv and from a future revision, and every non-lease, non-compaction error code.

Local runs on `bcf40d5`, this host: `scripts/difftest.sh etcd` passes, `scripts/difftest.sh tigerstore` passes with the expected failures above, two recordings in a row are byte-identical for both servers, and `golangci-lint run ./...` reports 0 issues.

title: Request size limit is 18 bytes looser than etcd v3.7.2
body:
Part of #47. Found by the differential tests against etcd v3.7.2 (branch `work/47-difftest`, `scripts/difftest.sh tigerstore`).

tigerstore accepts larger requests than etcd v3.7.2 with its default `--max-request-bytes` of 1.5 MiB. Measured locally on main `b8bac8b`, 3-node cluster from `scripts/local-cluster.sh`, against a fresh single-node etcd v3.7.2. The key is 39 bytes in both runs:

| Request | Largest value etcd v3.7.2 accepts | Largest value tigerstore accepts |
|---|---:|---:|
| Put | 1,572,801 bytes | 1,572,819 bytes |
| Txn with one Put | 1,572,793 bytes | 1,572,811 bytes |

Expected: one byte more than etcd's largest value fails with `InvalidArgument`, `etcdserver: request is too large`. Actual: tigerstore accepts up to 18 more bytes.

Cause, read from the code but not proven by a test: `internal/core/node.go` compares `proto.Size` of the client request with the limit. etcd compares the size of the marshaled `InternalRaftRequest`, which wraps the request with a header holding the request ID, plus the field tag and length. The ID comes from the member ID, so the size of the wrapper is fixed for one member.

The differential test `max-request-size` lists this as an expected failure until it is fixed.

title: Watch: core watchers, gRPC watch streams, simulated watch clients
body:
Part of #47

Fourth slice: Watch. Stacked on #59 (base `work/47-server`).

- `internal/core/watch.go`: watchers per stream, following etcd v3.7.2's watch server. Watch ID 0 picks the next free ID from 0; a taken ID or a negative start revision gets etcd's created-and-canceled answer with ID -1; a start below the compaction revision gets `CompactRevision` and a cancel. A watcher in the past catches up from `mvcc.Store.History` at once, in responses of at most 1,000 revisions that never split a revision. After each applied write the core matches its changes, and at the end of `Process` each watcher gets one response with the current revision as header. `prev_kv` from the key's version list (none on create), NOPUT and NODELETE filters, cancel, progress requests (always answered with ID -1, since every watcher is synced), and progress notifications every `ProgressTicks` (etcd's 10 minutes).
- `internal/node`: watch streams with a 4096-response queue; a stream that falls further behind is closed with `ResourceExhausted` and the client resumes.
- `internal/server/watch.go`: the Watch service, with etcd's `hasleader` metadata (refuse to open without a leader, close when the leader is gone at a 500 ms check). A client that closes its send side keeps getting responses, as in etcd.
- `internal/sim`: three watch clients (prefix with prev_kv, single key with prev_kv, open-ended without) that start from revision 1 or now, resume after crashes and also drop their stream on purpose about every 3 s and resume up to 2 s later. Each must deliver exactly the final store's history of its range from its start to the final revision, in order, without duplicates, with previous values. The workload now also has range deletes of up to 3 keys and transactions that put two keys, so one revision can carry several events.
- `scripts/smoke.sh`: etcdctl watch on a prefix sees put, put, delete.
- `docs/design.md` and README.

- 400 fresh seeds (5000 to 5399) pass, each replayed twice in one process; 32 seeds give identical trace files with default `GOMAXPROCS` and `GOMAXPROCS=1`.
- Planted by hand, each fails seed 1: events without previous values, a watcher that skips its history, a watcher that gets only the first change of each write, a watcher that starts one revision late.
- `TestWatchOverTLS`: watch with history and prev_kv on node 2 while node 1 writes, then a progress request. `go test -race` for `server` and `peer`, `golangci-lint` (0 issues), `go test -short ./...` and `scripts/smoke.sh` pass.

title: Real node: driver, TLS peer transport, etcd gRPC server, command
body:
Part of #47

Third slice, stacked on #58 (base `work/47-sim`; GitHub moves the base when #58 merges). This makes tigerstore a running 3-node cluster.

- `internal/node`: the real driver of `core.Node`. One committer goroutine owns the core: it waits for an input or a 100 ms tick, takes up to 4096 queued inputs, calls `Process` once and carries out the effects. One disk goroutine drains every queued persist job into one WAL write and one fsync (group commit). `Node.Do(ctx, op)` is what gRPC handlers call.
- `internal/peer`: the decided transport, framed TLS 1.3 over TCP behind `peer.Transport` (`Send`, `Close`). One outbound connection per peer, mutual certificate checks against the peer CA, an 8-byte ID preface, then 4-byte-length frames of `raftpb.Message`. Control messages go before entry messages; entry queue capped at 64 MiB, frames at 64 MiB, 5 s write deadline. `Send` never blocks: drops are reported to Raft as unreachable. The writer goroutine marshals, not the committer.
- `internal/server`: KV (Range, Put, DeleteRange, Txn) and Cluster.MemberList over client TLS with optional required client certificates; every other method returns Unimplemented. 1.5 MiB request limit plus etcd's 512 KiB gRPC room.
- `cmd/tigerstore` with etcd's flag names; peer URLs must be https. `scripts/dev-certs.sh`, `scripts/local-cluster.sh`, `scripts/smoke.sh`, and a README that shows how to start 3 nodes on one machine.
- CI: `smoke` job runs etcdctl v3.7.2 put, get (linearizable and serializable), del and range del against a local 3-node cluster over TLS, and checks that a client without a certificate is refused. Needed by `ci`.
- `docs/design.md`: the real node, transport, server and command, and seams for other transports, health and version on the client port, and backpressure.

Tests: `internal/peer` (ordered delivery, unreachable while a peer is down, reconnect, a node from another CA is refused) and `internal/server` (3 nodes in one process over real TLS: write on one node, linearizable read on another, CAS on a third, a request without key, restart of a node from disk with a read at a past revision and after a delete, a client certificate from another CA refused). Part of #47

Crashes with torn tails (crash between write and fsync), restarts from disk, 64 directed-link masks, ordered streams with delays, slow disks, 6 clients. Checks: replicas agree, every read matches the final store at its revision, acked writes and their previous values are in the final store, CAS compares held, revisions follow real time and writes get unique newer revisions, liveness 4 s after healing. Every event goes into a trace hash and `TestSeeds` replays each seed twice.

title: Storage: MVCC index, Raft log on disk, real and simulated disks
body:
Part of #47

First slice of the core: the storage pieces of one node. No server or Raft loop yet; the next PR adds the committer and the simulator on top.

- `internal/mvcc`: key index on a B-tree with every version per key. Range, Put, DeleteRange and Txn follow etcd v3.7.2 rule by rule (revision only moves when a key changes, Count ignores revision filters, limit pushdown only with the default order, compares read the state before the transaction, nested responses carry an empty header). Validation before a request enters the log is `mvcc.Check*` with etcd's `rpctypes` errors. `Store.Changes` and `Change.Event` feed watches later; `Store.Hash` lets the simulator compare replicas.
- `internal/wal`: the only durable copy of the data. Segment files of records with a chained CRC-32C. An entry record replaces the suffix from its index, so a truncation and its replacement are synced together. `Append` buffers, `Sync` does one write and one fsync. Recovery cuts a torn tail in the newest segment and returns `ErrCorrupt` for anything a crash cannot cause, including a commit index past the last entry.
- `internal/osfs` and `internal/simfs`: the real directory and a byte-level simulated disk with volatile and durable state, torn-tail crashes, erase, and a fault hook on every operation.
- `docs/design.md`: "What is built" and "Seams for later pieces".

Tests: etcd edge cases in `mvcc`, a 500-seed WAL crash test that crashes between write and fsync and checks recovery returns the synced log plus a prefix of unsynced records. I checked that the crash test fails when the torn-tail truncation or the crc check is removed.

title: Checkers over one plain history format
body:
Part of #47.

The checkers piece of #47: one plain history format in its own package (`history`), and four checkers in `check` that read it.

- `check.Linearizable` runs Porcupine v1.1.0 (the version etcd v3.7.2's robustness tests pin) with a port of etcd v3.7.2's robustness model (`tests/robustness/model`). It follows upstream's non-deterministic handling of ambiguous errors. The port adds create revisions, leases on keys, range deletes, every compare target and result, count-only and limited ranges, and the semantic errors (compacted, future revision, lease not found, lease exists). A timeout or deadline is a failure, never a pass.
- `check.Watches` is the strict watch checker. A watch that asks for previous values must get one on every update and delete event, equal to the replayed predecessor, and none on creates. Events are compared one by one against the replayed log from the watch's first revision up to `History.Target` for watches the server did not cancel. They must match the filter, be ordered, unique and atomic per revision. Progress notifications must come after all events at or below their revision. Nothing may arrive above the committed log. A compaction cancel must name a compacted revision above the next needed revision. When the watch asked for previous values, a cancel at exactly that revision is also allowed. etcd v3.7.2 sends such an event without `prev_kv`, and Kubernetes rejects that event.
- `check.Durable` checks that every acked mutation that changed the store is in the recovered log with the response the client got. Every successful read, the final scans included, must match the log at its revision. Every log entry that changed the store must be a request some client sent, used at most once. An unclaimed `LeaseRevoke` is a lease expiry.
- `check.Revisions` checks the revision rules on the client view alone: KV field sanity, real-time order of header revisions (strict for writes), one revision per write, keys at a write's revision hold what that write put, versions reset on recreate, and compacted and future errors only where they can be right.

Each checker has tests with good histories and deliberately broken ones. Every broken history must fail, and must fail for the stated reason (the test matches the error text). `TestModel` pins the model to etcd behaviour written out by hand. That behaviour includes what etcd v3.7.2 returned in my local differential runs: revision 0 or less reads the current revision, a read at the compaction revision works, compacting there again fails, and lease grant only checks the ID because etcd raises short TTLs.

## The history format

`history/history.go` is the format. The simulator and the real-process harness both write it.

- `History.Ops` are client calls with call and return times from one clock, the request, and either the response or an error. An error with `Ambiguous` set may or may not have taken effect, at any time after the call.
- `History.Watches` are client watch streams with every response the client received. A watch without a start revision must record its created response.
- `History.Log` is the committed log in commit order, as plain requests, with lease expiry as `LeaseRevoke` and lease grants with their ID. The watch and durability checkers replay it through the ported model, not through tigerstore code.
- `History.Target` is a revision the harness got after mutations stopped.

## Not in this PR

The sequential differential tests against etcd v3.7.2 (compaction at R-1, R and R+1, error codes, maximum request size) follow in a separate PR. They run locally against a downloaded etcd v3.7.2 and record its answers. CI wiring and a re-record are left.

title: Core layout on the runner
body:
Part of [Map: tigerstore, a faster etcd for Kubernetes](https://github.com/djosh34/tigerstore/issues/1).

## Question
How are the runner's 4 cores laid out in benchmarks?

## Context
[Benchmark venue](/31) gave one pinned core per replica and one for the generator. [Owner design directions](https://github.com/djosh34/tigerstore/issues/53) wants helper threads to prepare work so the committer core never blocks. With one core per replica, those helpers share the committer's core, so that part of the design cannot show on the runner. Three runners cannot easily reach each other.

## Options
A. Keep one pinned core per replica and one for the generator. The helper-thread gain shows only in CPU per op, not in throughput, on the runner.
B. The architect may choose the core layout per benchmark (for example the leader gets 2 cores, followers share 1, generator 1), as long as etcd runs with the identical layout in the same job and the layout is reported with the numbers.
C. All processes unpinned on 4 shared cores.

## Recommendation
B.

title: Brutal real-process chaos
body:
Part of [Map: tigerstore, a faster etcd for Kubernetes](https://github.com/djosh34/tigerstore/issues/1). Outcome issue 3 of 6, after [Real Kubernetes on tigerstore](https://github.com/djosh34/tigerstore/issues/48). Follow [Playbook: run plan 1](https://github.com/djosh34/tigerstore/issues/46).

## Goal

Real tigerstore processes survive brutal faults with every guarantee intact, and a red team has failed to break them.

## Done when

- Our own seeded Go fault proxy sits on every link (client to node, node to node). It can drop, delay (short, long, switching), stall, reset, corrupt and duplicate bytes, cut one direction or both, and make one link much faster than another. ([Test layers](https://github.com/djosh34/tigerstore/issues/20))
- Real-process chaos jobs combine the proxy with tc netem (packet loss, reordering, corruption), SIGKILL and SIGSTOP, CPU throttling, a fault-injecting file layer (torn writes, failing and stalling fsync, disk full), crashes during WAL recovery and snapshot install, gray nodes and barely-alive clients with numeric liveness bounds, and 1 to 10 ms between nodes. ([Single region](https://github.com/djosh34/tigerstore/issues/29), [Starting test design](https://github.com/djosh34/tigerstore/issues/33))
- The linearizability, watch and durability checkers run on every chaos history; a job fails if a requested fault was not installed.
- Short chaos jobs run on every PR in `ci`; long campaigns run nightly as many short jobs.
- At least 3 red-team rounds by fresh GPT-6 Astra agents ran against `main` (chaos only, no security work), every break they found is fixed with a regression test, and no `bug` issue from the red team is open. ([Red team](https://github.com/djosh34/tigerstore/issues/36))
- Merged as the playbook says.

title: Correct core under deterministic simulation
body:
Part of [Map: tigerstore, a faster etcd for Kubernetes](https://github.com/djosh34/tigerstore/issues/1). Outcome issue 1 of 6. Follow [Playbook: run plan 1](https://github.com/djosh34/tigerstore/issues/46).

## Goal

tigerstore runs as a 3-node cluster on go.etcd.io/raft with its own storage, serves the etcd API that kube-apiserver uses, and the whole cluster runs in a seeded deterministic simulator that tries hard to break it.

## Done when

- Go module `github.com/djosh34/tigerstore` on Go 1.27 with one executable `tigerstore` that runs one node; the README shows how to start a 3-node cluster on one machine. ([Implementation language](https://github.com/djosh34/tigerstore/issues/9), [Deployment shape](https://github.com/djosh34/tigerstore/issues/11))
- It serves Range (single key, prefix, limit, count, keys-only, at a revision), Txn with MOD and VERSION compares and the failure-branch Range, Put with lease, DeleteRange, Watch (start revision, prev_kv, progress notify, RequestProgress, compaction errors, require-leader), LeaseGrant with expiry, Compact, Maintenance.Status reporting etcd version 3.7.x, MemberList, and returns Unimplemented for RangeStream. Client TLS with client certificates works. GET `/health` and `/version` work over TLS on the client port (kubeadm's preflight checks `/version`), and a CI smoke test runs etcdctl get, put, del, watch and endpoint status against it over TLS. ([etcd semantics k8s needs](https://github.com/djosh34/tigerstore/issues/3), [Compatibility scope](https://github.com/djosh34/tigerstore/issues/7), [Supported versions](https://github.com/djosh34/tigerstore/issues/18))
- There is no bbolt in `go.mod`, and `docs/design.md` describes what is built, starting from the merged design, including the Raft log as the value store. Node-to-node traffic is encrypted. ([Starting design](https://github.com/djosh34/tigerstore/issues/32), [Design changes](https://github.com/djosh34/tigerstore/issues/37))
- `docs/design.md` follows the [Owner design directions](https://github.com/djosh34/tigerstore/issues/53): a single-threaded committer that owns all state without locks and is fed prepared batches by helper threads, responses prepared before commit and released at commit, a node-to-node transport chosen by measurement (no gRPC or protobuf required between nodes, encrypted), and an explicit analysis of how batch size follows load and node-to-node latency.
- The simulator runs the real core of all 3 nodes in one process from one seed, with stock raft v3.7.0 made deterministic by `testing/cryptotest.SetGlobalRandom`; every PR replays seeds twice and compares trace hashes; a lint stops core packages from using wall time, global randomness, syscalls or goroutines. ([Starting test design](https://github.com/djosh34/tigerstore/issues/33))
- The simulator injects every fault in the starting test design (byte-level disk faults, crashes at every persistence step including during WAL recovery and snapshot install, stream network faults with all 64 link masks and switching, asymmetric and switching delays, gray nodes and clients with numeric liveness bounds, pauses, clock skew and jumps), and checks linearizability (Porcupine on isolated small histories) and acked-write durability under those faults, the strict watch checker (previous value required on updates and deletes, not on creates), durability including erase-one-disk cold restarts, and revision rules. ([Starting test design](https://github.com/djosh34/tigerstore/issues/33))
- Every planted bug (behind a test-only build tag) is caught within its fixed seed budget, in CI. ([Starting test design](https://github.com/djosh34/tigerstore/issues/33))
- Sequential differential tests against etcd v3.7.2 pass for the boundaries listed in the starting test design.
- GitHub Actions on free runners, many short jobs, with lint as the playbook lists and the required aggregate check `ci` (fails if any job fails) on every PR, and branch protection on `main` requires `ci`. ([Load generator and speed metrics](https://github.com/djosh34/tigerstore/issues/45), [Test layers](https://github.com/djosh34/tigerstore/issues/20))
- Merged as the playbook says.

title: Playbook: run plan 1
body:
Part of [Map: tigerstore, a faster etcd for Kubernetes](https://github.com/djosh34/tigerstore/issues/1). Decided in [Plan outcomes and their order](https://github.com/djosh34/tigerstore/issues/34).

# Playbook

Every agent of this plan reads this first, then the map #1 and the outcome issue it works on. Where sources disagree, the outcome issue and the newest owner answer win over older decision tickets, and decision tickets win over this playbook. `docs/design.md` on `main` is the current design; the architect may change it (see Architect).

## Start

The owner pastes this line into a fresh Opus 5.5 paseo agent:

> You are the architect of tigerstore plan 1. Work in /home/joshazimullah.linux/work_mounts/tigerstore. Read the playbook issue #46 and the map issue #1 of djosh34/tigerstore with gh, then run the plan until it is done or paused.

Same thing from a shell:

```sh
cd /home/joshazimullah.linux/work_mounts/tigerstore
paseo run -d --provider claude/claude-opus-5-5 --thinking high --mode bypassPermissions \
  --title "tigerstore plan 1: architect" --label plan=1 --label role=architect \
  "<the line above>"
```

If the architect dies, the owner pastes the same line again. The new architect picks up from GitHub and `paseo ls -g --label plan=1`. To resume after the pause, the owner pastes the same line with "New deadline: <time>" appended; without a new deadline a resumed architect only posts a status report and stops.

## Deadline and pause

The deadline is **2026-10-13T22:00:00Z** (Wednesday 2026-10-14 00:00 Europe/Amsterdam). Opus 5.5 usage resets then, so use it fully until the deadline. Every worker and helper prompt states the deadline; each agent checks the time before starting new work or merging, and starts or merges nothing at or after it. At the deadline the plan pauses:

1. Start nothing new and merge nothing more. Every worker pushes its branch first (`paseo send --no-wait`, then wait at most 10 minutes).
2. `paseo delete` every agent of the plan except the architect; remove their worktrees.
3. Post a "Paused" report on the map: what is merged, the latest tag, the benchmark table against etcd, open bugs and branches, and what the next steps would be.
4. Delete the heartbeat and stop. Leave the map, this playbook and the open outcome issues open.

## Architect

- Runs the 6 outcome issues in order. An outcome closes only when every line of its "Done when" holds on `main`.
- Owns large architecture decisions (for example storage format, transport, index, checkpointing, threading). Before deciding one, it asks a fresh GPT-6 Astra agent for a second opinion, and records the decision and evidence in a "Design change" comment on the current outcome issue and in `docs/design.md` (through a worker's PR). Workers decide small design choices themselves and message the architect only for large ones. Owner-fixed items never change: etcd v3 API as kube-apiserver uses it plus TLS, go.etcd.io/raft, Go, one executable per node, 3 nodes in one region, encrypted node-to-node traffic, linearizable reads and writes, acked writes survive loss of one node, free GitHub runners, red team chaos only.
- Starts with one worker that lands the skeleton: `go.mod` (Go 1.27), the `ci` workflow with lint, branch protection on `main` requiring `ci`, and `docs/design.md` from [#32](https://github.com/djosh34/tigerstore/issues/32), [#33](https://github.com/djosh34/tigerstore/issues/33) and [#53](https://github.com/djosh34/tigerstore/issues/53). Other workers start after it merges. Test gates join `ci` as they get built.
- Then runs up to 3 Opus 5.5 workers at once: on the current outcome and on independent pieces of later outcomes (for example the fault proxy, the load generator, the Kubernetes test adapter, the release workflow). Each piece has its own branch and PR, which says `Part of #<n>` of the outcome it belongs to, and merges as soon as it is green and reviewed. "In order" applies to closing outcome issues, not to merging pieces.
- Is the only one who starts GPT-6 Astra agents (at most 4 running at once). Workers that want one ask it with one short message.
- Uses `paseo send --no-wait` for every message, so it never blocks.
- After starting the first worker, creates its own heartbeat, keeps its ID and posts the ID as a comment on this playbook: `paseo heartbeat create --cron '*/30 * * * *' --timezone Europe/Amsterdam --name check-workers "Check the workers and the deadline as the playbook says."` This heartbeat is the only watchdog.
- On each heartbeat: first, if the time is at or past the deadline, pause. Otherwise look at the workers with `paseo ls -g --label plan=1`, `paseo logs <id>`, and the GitHub activity of their branches and PRs. Nothing else.
  - **Worker stopped:** it ended, errored, or sits idle with its task unfinished. Wake it at once with `paseo send --no-wait`. A worker waiting on CI, a review, an Astra slot or another piece is not stopped.
  - **Worker silent:** no commit, push, PR activity or log output for 60 minutes, not counting a wait on a rate or usage limit. Nudge it once.
  - **Still nothing after 30 more minutes:** `paseo delete` it, remove its worktree, and start a replacement (commands below). The replacement continues from what is on GitHub.
  - **Fewer than 3 Opus workers busy:** start more on the next pieces, while Opus usage lasts.
- **When a worker reports done:**
  - For a piece: checks that its PR is merged, deletes the worker and starts the next one. A merged piece does not close its outcome.
  - For an outcome: checks every line of its "Done when" on `main`, closes it with a short summary comment that mentions @djosh34, deletes the worker and starts the next one.
- **A huge blocker from a worker:** the architect decides it by the map's notes and decisions, and writes the decision as a comment on the outcome issue. Only when it truly cannot go on, for example a service is down for good or a credential fails, does it tell the owner in a comment that mentions @djosh34, then continues with any other work that is possible.
- Writes no code and never relays details between agents.
- Outcome 6 never finishes before the deadline: the plan always ends in the pause.

Starting a worker:

```sh
git -C /home/joshazimullah.linux/work_mounts/tigerstore fetch origin
paseo run -d --provider claude/claude-opus-5-5 --thinking high --mode bypassPermissions \
  --cwd /home/joshazimullah.linux/work_mounts/tigerstore --new-workspace worktree --worktree-mode branch-off --new-branch work/<n>-<slug> --base origin/main \
  --title "tigerstore 1 worker <n> <slug>" --label plan=1 --label role=worker --label issue=<n> \
  "You are a worker for outcome issue #<n> of tigerstore plan 1. Your task: <task>. Deadline: 2026-10-13T22:00:00Z; start and merge nothing after it. Read the playbook issue #46, the map #1 and issue #<n> with its comments, then finish your task. Message the architect <architect id> with paseo send --no-wait only when done, for a huge blocker, a large architecture decision or an Astra request."
```

`<task>` is either "finish the outcome to its Done when" or one named piece. The architect fills `<architect id>` with its own ID from `$PASEO_AGENT_ID`. `<slug>` is new for every worker; a replacement after a merge gets a new slug such as `<slug>-2`.

Replacing a worker on an existing branch: first remove the old worker's worktree and its local branch (`git -C /home/joshazimullah.linux/work_mounts/tigerstore worktree remove --force <old path>` and `git -C /home/joshazimullah.linux/work_mounts/tigerstore branch -D work/<n>-<slug>`), so the replacement gets what was pushed. Then:

```sh
git -C /home/joshazimullah.linux/work_mounts/tigerstore fetch origin
paseo run -d --provider claude/claude-opus-5-5 --thinking high --mode bypassPermissions \
  --cwd /home/joshazimullah.linux/work_mounts/tigerstore --new-workspace worktree --worktree-mode checkout-branch --branch work/<n>-<slug> \
  --title "tigerstore 1 worker <n> <slug>" --label plan=1 --label role=worker --label issue=<n> \
  "You replace a worker for outcome issue #<n> of tigerstore plan 1. Your task: <task>. Deadline: 2026-10-13T22:00:00Z; start and merge nothing after it. Read the playbook issue #46, the map #1, issue #<n> with its comments and the open PR of branch work/<n>-<slug>, then finish your task. Push with git push -u origin HEAD. Message the architect <architect id> with paseo send --no-wait only when done, for a huge blocker, a large architecture decision or an Astra request."
```

Replacing a worker after its PR is merged: start the replacement with the "Starting a worker" command and a new slug, and tell it in the prompt that the PR is merged. It reads the merged PR and does only the steps that are left. If a release tag already exists, it never creates or moves it again.

## Worker

- Owns its task until it holds on `main`. It decides how.
- Messages the architect with `paseo send --no-wait`, only with "done" and the PR links, a huge blocker, a large architecture decision with its evidence, or an Astra request. Everything else it decides itself, by the map's decisions and `docs/design.md`.
- Pushes after every meaningful step.
- Before each push, runs `test -z "$(gofmt -l .)" && go vet ./... && golangci-lint run ./... && go test -short ./...` for the packages it changed. CI runs the full check.
- Waits on CI with a background loop (polling every 2 minutes at most) and keeps working on the next part meanwhile, instead of ending its turn.

## Helpers: Astra and Sol

- **Only Opus 5.5 writes code that merges to `main`.**
- GPT-6 Astra agents do ideas, second opinions, PR review, the red team and throwaway experiments (a quick prototype or microbenchmark that tells whether an idea is worth an Opus worker). Only the architect starts them, at most **4 running at once**, with `paseo run -d --provider pi/openai-codex/gpt-6-astra --thinking high --label plan=1 --label model=astra --label role=<role> ...`, with the deadline and "Do not create subagents." in the prompt.
- GPT-6.1 Sol agents are unlimited: any agent may start them for research and experiments on its own part, with `paseo run -d --provider pi/openai-codex/gpt-6.1-sol --thinking high --label plan=1 --label model=sol ...`, with the deadline in the prompt.
- Helpers work in their own directory (`--cwd` of a fresh folder, or their own worktree on a branch `exp/<slug>`), never in a worker's checkout. Throwaway code is never merged.
- Helpers post their results as comments on the outcome issue or PR they serve, and are deleted right after.
- An agent that fails on a cybersecurity flag is deleted at once, and that path or prompt is never retried.
- If Opus hits its usage limit before the deadline, Opus agents wait for the reset. Astra and Sol keep running experiments and red-team rounds and post results for when Opus is back.

## Tournament (outcomes 4 and 6)

- Each round the architect picks 2 to 3 bold ideas from the speed-of-light numbers in `docs/performance.md` and the helpers' experiments, and starts one Opus worker per idea, each on its own branch `work/<n>-<idea>`. Whole components may be thrown away and rewritten.
- Every branch runs the same small benchmark set (for example Put and CAS Txn at 1 KiB, 0 and 5 ms between nodes): the lean load generator against etcd 3.7.2, the current `main` and the branch, back to back in the same runner job, with disk write barriers on, 5 repetitions, server CPU per op reported. The full matrix runs for releases and when the architect asks. The architect picks the core layout per benchmark (for example leader 2 cores, followers sharing 1, generator 1); etcd always gets the identical layout, and the layout is reported with the numbers ([Core layout on the runner](https://github.com/djosh34/tigerstore/issues/54)).
- The benchmark set also has a varied workload, not only fixed keys and fixed values: creates, updates, deletes, LISTs and watches mixed; Kubernetes-shaped keys over a key space that grows to at least 1M; value sizes drawn from a real Kubernetes object dump; clients spread over all three nodes; open-loop arrivals. Every result reports its spread over the repetitions (min, median, max), not one number. A kube-burner run on kind (create, update and mass-delete churn) compares both stores at the Kubernetes level, 3 runs each, with the same spread. (Owner instruction, 2026-10-13T15:05Z.)
- Now and then the same benchmark also runs on this host (8 cores, so more cores per replica), labelled as host results, with nothing else heavy running at the same time.
- Winners merge one at a time: `gh pr update-branch`, rerun every gate, merge. In outcome 6, merged improvements are then released as the next tag. A loser gets a comment with its numbers on the outcome issue and its PR is closed; its branch stays on GitHub and its local worktree is deleted.
- A benchmark regression, a failing gate or an open red-team break blocks every merge except the PR that fixes it.
- Every round's numbers, wins and losses, go on the outcome issue and into `docs/performance.md`.

## Red team

- In outcomes 3, 4 and 6, after every merged change to the core, storage, transport or recovery, a fresh GPT-6 Astra red-team agent tries to break `main`: new fault schedules, seeds, nasty but legal client behaviour, gray nodes and clients, crash timings. Never security work: no exploits, no attacks on binaries or protocols, no security fuzzing. Only chaos for durability and correctness.
- Each break becomes an issue labelled `bug` with the seed or script and the expected and actual behaviour, made a sub-issue of the outcome issue with `gh api repos/djosh34/tigerstore/issues/<outcome>/sub_issues -F sub_issue_id=$(gh api repos/djosh34/tigerstore/issues/<bug> --jq .id)`. An Opus worker fixes it and adds the regression test at the layer that reproduces it (simulator scenario where possible). No outcome closes while a red-team break is open.
- The architect may close a red-team bug as not a bug, with the evidence in a comment (for example the same script against etcd 3.7.2 behaves the same).
- Part of outcome 3 (#49): Jepsen's etcd test ([jepsen-io/etcd](https://github.com/jepsen-io/etcd)) and the traffic and checkers of etcd's own robustness tests (`go.etcd.io/etcd/tests/robustness`) run against a 3-node tigerstore on free GitHub runners, with partitions, kills, pauses and clock faults, and their failures are filed as `bug` sub-issues of #49 like red-team breaks. Where a check depends on an etcd-only mechanism (for example gofail failpoints), the job says so and uses our fault proxy or file layer instead. (Owner instruction, 2026-10-13T15:58Z.)

## Tags and releases

- The release workflow is started by hand (`workflow_dispatch`) with the version. It cuts the tag from a green `main`, builds the binaries and the image, and makes the GitHub release, in one run.
- `v0.1.0` is made by outcome 5. After that, merged improvements in outcome 6 are released as `v0.1.1`, `v0.1.2`, and so on, with the benchmark numbers against etcd and against the previous tag in the notes. One tag may cover several merged improvements.

## CI

- Free GitHub-hosted runners only (`ubuntu-24.04-arm`, also `ubuntu-24.04` for the amd64 build). CI installs Go 1.27.
- One test or benchmark per runner job, many jobs in parallel. Prefer many short jobs (aim for 15 minutes or less each) and let GitHub queue them over few long jobs.
- The aggregate required check on every PR is named `ci`. It runs with `if: always()` and fails unless every job it needs succeeded. Nightly and release-only workflows are separate and can also be started by hand.
- Lint with `golangci-lint`: errcheck, errorlint, nilerr, forbidigo (no `panic`, `recover` or stray `fmt.Print`), govet, staticcheck, ineffassign, wastedassign, unused, unparam, durationcheck, copyloopvar, exhaustive, gocritic, modernize, unconvert, usestdlibvars, perfsprint, misspell, gofumpt, and nolintlint (every `//nolint` names its linter and gives a reason). A linter that proves to need too many `//nolint` comments is removed from the set instead. Linters only keep the default code clean: breaking them for measured performance is encouraged, with a `//nolint` whose reason names the gain.

## PRs

- Branch from `origin/main`. One PR per task.
- The PR body says `Part of #<n>`. Never `Closes`, `Fixes` or `Resolves`: only the architect closes outcome issues.
- **Reviewers per PR:**
  - Outcomes 1 to 5: one Opus 5.5 reviewer with fresh context, looking for bugs and slop (a large PR may get several, one per part of the code): `paseo run -d --provider claude/claude-opus-5-5 --thinking high --mode bypassPermissions --cwd /home/joshazimullah.linux/work_mounts/tigerstore --new-workspace worktree --worktree-mode checkout-pr --pr-number <pr> --title "tigerstore 1 opus review <pr>" --label plan=1 --label role=reviewer "<brief>"`, and one GPT-6 Astra reviewer, started by the architect on the worker's request: `paseo run -d --provider pi/openai-codex/gpt-6-astra --thinking high --cwd /home/joshazimullah.linux/work_mounts/tigerstore --new-workspace worktree --worktree-mode checkout-pr --pr-number <pr> --title "tigerstore 1 astra review <pr>" --label plan=1 --label model=astra --label role=reviewer "<brief>"`.
  - Outcome 6: only the Astra reviewer, focused on correctness and durability.
  - The brief: review PR <pr> of djosh34/tigerstore with the `pr-review` skill and post the findings as one PR comment. Do not create subagents.
- **Review rounds:**
  - The worker fixes what it agrees with and answers the rest in one line. Review comments that push toward overengineering are ignored.
  - When anything was fixed, the reviewers check only the fixes, once, each with a PR comment. No merge before every reviewer's comment is there. More rounds happen only when that check finds a real bug.
  - Reviewers are deleted after their fix check, with their worktrees.
- **Merge** when CI is green and the reviews are handled: `gh pr update-branch <pr>`, wait for `ci`, then `gh pr merge <pr> --repo djosh34/tigerstore --squash --delete-branch`. `--repo` stops gh from checking out `main` in the worker's worktree. A tournament loser's branch is not deleted.

## Rules

- **Fast.** Make it wicked fast. Reason from what one core can do, think outside the box, try ideas others call crazy. The guarantees never bend.
- **Brutal tests.** Assume bugs exist. A test that never fails is a broken test. A checker timeout, a skipped check or a fault that was not installed is a failure.
- **Simple.** Keep the code simple and well written. No slop, no overengineering. The owner must be able to read and use every file.
- **Errors.** No panic or recover in our code. An ignored error or a reachable crash is a defect.
- **Writing.** Every issue, PR, commit message, comment and doc follows `~/.agents/skills/unslop/SKILL.md` (read the file; it is not loadable as a skill).
- **Git.** Never push to `main` directly, never rebase or force-push a branch with an open PR, never delete or move a tag. Only the release workflow creates tags.
- **CI.** Use REST `gh api` calls. Check CI with `gh api repos/djosh34/tigerstore/commits/<sha>/check-runs` or `gh run view`, no faster than every 2 minutes, never with `--watch`.
- **Usage.** When Opus usage runs out, wait for the reset. Never switch to another model for writing code that merges.
- **Issues:**
  - Agents may comment on the outcome issue they work on and open `bug` issues. The architect closes outcome issues; the map and this playbook stay open at the pause.
  - No agent edits or closes the decision tickets or the map body.
- **Reports.** State evidence: what ran, on which commit, with what result. A green rerun shows the rerun passed, not that the first failure was harmless. A cause that was not proven is written as a guess, and an open defect stays named as open. Benchmark claims name the runner, core layout, generator, repetitions and the etcd baseline measured in the same job.
- **Notes.** Notes, evidence, reports and decisions go on GitHub, as issue or PR comments. Never leave them only in local files, in the home directory or in `/tmp`.
- **Cleanup.** Delete the worktrees of deleted agents. Keep an eye on disk space and delete build output of finished work.
- **Approvals.** Avoid any action that would need the owner to approve it, even in bypass mode. Find another way, or report it as a blocker.
- **Public repo.** No secrets in code, logs or comments.

title: Load generator and speed metrics
body:
Part of [Map: tigerstore, a faster etcd for Kubernetes](https://github.com/djosh34/tigerstore/issues/1).

## Question
Which load generator and metrics judge speed?

## Context
On a free 4-CPU runner with one pinned core per replica, the load generator gets one core. etcd's own benchmark tool uses grpc-go, which costs about 17 to 29 us of CPU per call ([#32](https://github.com/djosh34/tigerstore/issues/32), [#28](https://github.com/djosh34/tigerstore/issues/28)), so one core can drive only a few tens of thousands of requests/s. That caps any store's measured throughput. Runners cannot easily reach each other, so the generator must share the runner. The Kubernetes-level tests (kube-burner, ClusterLoader2) are bound by the apiserver anyway.

## Options
A. Write our own lean load generator: raw HTTP/2 gRPC client, many streams per connection, prebuilt requests, open-loop arrivals with recorded latency, CAS, Put, Delete, Range and Watch workloads, Kubernetes-shaped keys. Drive both etcd 3.7.2 and tigerstore with it. Also report server CPU microseconds per operation, which shows efficiency even when the generator is the limit. Keep etcd's own benchmark tool numbers as a second, standard view.
B. Only etcd's benchmark tool.
C. A, and the architect may give the generator 2 cores by putting the 3 replicas on 2 cores when that shows more.

## Recommendation
A. Same generator for both stores keeps it fair; server CPU per op keeps it honest.

title: Improvement tags and pause
body:
Part of [Map: tigerstore, a faster etcd for Kubernetes](https://github.com/djosh34/tigerstore/issues/1).

## Question
How are improvement tags numbered, and what does "pause" at the deadline do?

## Context
[Deadline and releases](https://github.com/djosh34/tigerstore/issues/40): v0.1.0 for the first working release, a new tag per merged improvement, the deadline is a pause.

## Options
A. Improvements are v0.1.1, v0.1.2, ... Each tag is a full GitHub release made by the release workflow (binaries, image), with that improvement's benchmark numbers against etcd in the notes. title: Done when for the speed outcome
body:
Part of [Map: tigerstore, a faster etcd for Kubernetes](https://github.com/djosh34/tigerstore/issues/1).

## Question
When is the speed outcome done?

## Context
Owner instruction, round 6: the plan runs fully autonomous while the owner is away. Keep it small and under-specified. The design may change during the plan. Hard instruction: make it wicked fast, think outside the box, do crazy things, boil the ocean. Test it brutally and try to break it, not kindly. The manager must check "Done when" itself. B. Relative to the derived bound: reach at least 50% of the single-core bound for Put, CAS and Delete, plus beat etcd on every headline metric, same stop rule.
C. No numeric target, only the stop rule.

## Recommendation
B. It forces the work towards what the hardware can do, not just past etcd, and the stop rule keeps the plan from running forever.

What are the outcome issues of the plan, in which order?
