title: Design: deterministic simulation and chaos testing
body:
Part of [Map: tigerstore, a faster etcd for Kubernetes](https://github.com/djosh34/tigerstore/issues/1).

## Question
How do we test tigerstore so hard that bugs have nowhere to hide, in TigerBeetle's style?

## Context
Fixed by the owner: etcd v3 API as kube-apiserver uses it plus TLS ([#3](https://github.com/djosh34/tigerstore/issues/3), [#7](https://github.com/djosh34/tigerstore/issues/7)), consensus with go.etcd.io/raft, fully new custom storage, Go, one executable per node, 3 nodes in one region, linearizable reads and writes, acked writes survive loss of one node ([#8](https://github.com/djosh34/tigerstore/issues/8)). No TigerBeetle. Goals in order: max number of objects, max throughput, latency equal or lower than etcd. Measured facts: [#26](https://github.com/djosh34/tigerstore/issues/26) (etcd profile: CPU-bound, gRPC plus protobuf about half the leader CPU), [#28](https://github.com/djosh34/tigerstore/issues/28) (primitive costs on a 4-CPU ARM runner), [#27](https://github.com/djosh34/tigerstore/issues/27) (k8s mass deletes), [#15](https://github.com/djosh34/tigerstore/issues/15) (value durability and group commit ideas, written for TigerBeetle but the byte path ideas carry over).

Decided in [Test layers and the release gate](https://github.com/djosh34/tigerstore/issues/20): our own seeded Go fault proxy on every link plus tc netem, apiserver storage tests through an adapter, the etcd linearizability checker (Porcupine) ported, full Kubernetes conformance, chaos with the checker running, all gating the release. TigerBeetle tests itself with deterministic simulation (VOPR): the whole cluster in one process with simulated network, disk, clock and crashes, driven by one seed, so every failure replays exactly. go.etcd.io/raft is a deterministic library without I/O, which may make the same possible here.

## Options
Two independent designs (GPT-6 Astra and Opus 5.5), then each answers the other.

## Recommendation
A design comment with: how the code must be structured so the whole cluster runs deterministically in one process (I/O, time and randomness behind small interfaces, single-threaded core); the simulator (network faults, disk faults such as torn writes, lost fsyncs, corruption, misdirected writes, crashes and restarts, clock skew); the checkers (linearizability, durability of acked writes, watch order and completeness, revision rules, invariants inside the state machine); how real-process chaos and Kubernetes tests complement it; what runs on every PR, nightly and before release on GitHub Actions; and how a failing seed becomes a regression test. No more machinery than needed.

title: Design: core store from single-core limits
body:
Part of [Map: tigerstore, a faster etcd for Kubernetes](https://github.com/djosh34/tigerstore/issues/1).

## Question
What is the design of tigerstore's core, derived from what one CPU core can do at most?

## Context
Fixed by the owner: etcd v3 API as kube-apiserver uses it plus TLS ([#3](https://github.com/djosh34/tigerstore/issues/3), [#7](https://github.com/djosh34/tigerstore/issues/7)), consensus with go.etcd.io/raft, fully new custom storage, Go, one executable per node, 3 nodes in one region, linearizable reads and writes, acked writes survive loss of one node ([#8](https://github.com/djosh34/tigerstore/issues/8)). No TigerBeetle. Goals in order: max number of objects, max throughput, latency equal or lower than etcd. Measured facts: [#26](https://github.com/djosh34/tigerstore/issues/26) (etcd profile: CPU-bound, gRPC plus protobuf about half the leader CPU), [#28](https://github.com/djosh34/tigerstore/issues/28) (primitive costs on a 4-CPU ARM runner), [#27](https://github.com/djosh34/tigerstore/issues/27) (k8s mass deletes), [#15](https://github.com/djosh34/tigerstore/issues/15) (value durability and group commit ideas, written for TigerBeetle but the byte path ideas carry over).

The owner's method: start from the hardware, not from etcd. How many operations per second can one thread do for each step of a write, read and watch (gRPC and HTTP/2 framing, protobuf decode and encode, key lookup and insert in an ordered index, memcpy, hashing, appending to a log, one fsync per batch, Raft bookkeeping per batch)? From that derive an upper bound for Put, CAS Txn, Delete, Range and Watch at 1 KiB and 10 KiB, for one client and for many. Then design so the hot path gets close to that bound: single-threaded core, batching everywhere, static or pooled memory, no per-request goroutine hops, possibly a custom gRPC and HTTP/2 server instead of grpc-go, multicore only where it does not add coordination. Kubernetes speaks unary gRPC per request, so per-request protocol cost is part of the bound.

## Options
Two independent designs (GPT-6 Astra and Opus 5.5), then each answers the other.

## Recommendation
A design comment with: the per-core numbers (measured with small Go benchmarks where possible), the derived upper bounds and which resource sets each; the architecture (threads, what runs where, what is batched); data structures and their memory per key; write, read, watch, lease and compaction paths; how Raft log, snapshots and the custom storage fit together; recovery after crash; max objects for a given RAM and disk; expected numbers on 3 separate machines and on one 4-CPU runner; the biggest risks and the first experiments. Keep it simple: the least machinery that reaches the bound.

title: Benchmark venue that can show a large gain
body:
Part of [Map: tigerstore, a faster etcd for Kubernetes on TigerBeetle](https://github.com/djosh34/tigerstore/issues/1). Revisits [Benchmark scale on GitHub runners](https://github.com/djosh34/tigerstore/issues/19).

## Question
Can the benchmark venue show a large gain at all?

## Context
On one free 4-CPU runner, 3 replicas and the load generator share 4 cores and one disk. [Hardware limits](https://github.com/djosh34/tigerstore/issues/28) puts the ceiling at about 2x etcd's measured throughput there, so even a perfect store can only show about 2x. Separate machines remove the shared-CPU cap: each replica gets its own cores and disk, and the leader's work is the limit. Larger GitHub-hosted runners (8 to 64 cores) cost money per minute; 3 separate cloud VMs cost a little per hour.

## Options
A. Keep free runners only; claim at most about 2x, labelled.
B. Free runners for CI, plus a paid larger runner (for example 16 or 32 cores, replicas pinned to separate cores) for the official numbers.
C. Free runners for CI, plus 3 cheap cloud VMs for the official numbers.

## Recommendation
B. It stays inside GitHub Actions, is scriptable, and costs a few euros per release run.

title: Route to a faster etcd: TigerBeetle, new Raft store, or etcd fork
body:
Part of [Map: tigerstore, a faster etcd for Kubernetes on TigerBeetle](https://github.com/djosh34/tigerstore/issues/1). Supersedes [TigerBeetle or another log, given growth and packaging facts](https://github.com/djosh34/tigerstore/issues/25).

## Question
Which route to a faster etcd with the same resilience?

## Context
- [Why etcd is slow](https://github.com/djosh34/tigerstore/issues/26): etcd already batches fsyncs. It is CPU-bound in per-request work: gRPC plus protobuf are about half the leader's CPU, disabling fsync gains only 7.5%. 27k Put/s at 1,024 clients, 0.79 ms at 1 client on a 4-CPU runner.
- [Hardware limits](https://github.com/djosh34/tigerstore/issues/28): on that same runner the ceiling is about 57k Put/s at 1 KiB and about 0.43 ms at 1 client. So any store, ours included, can be at most about 2x etcd there. The gap is larger on real separate machines and for object count, where etcd's bbolt, MVCC history and 2 GiB quota bite.
- [Mass deletes](https://github.com/djosh34/tigerstore/issues/27): Kubernetes deletes a namespace one object at a time with 1 worker and 2 etcd round trips per object. Raising --delete-collection-workers to 16 made 50k deletes 3.3 to 3.6x faster on unchanged etcd.
- [Design: etcd semantics on stock TigerBeetle](https://github.com/djosh34/tigerstore/issues/14): workable as a batch log, growth still unbounded, needs epoch rotation.
- A fork of etcd keeps etcd's own robustness, integration and e2e suites working unchanged, which is most of the testing the owner asked for. Its gains are capped by its structure: one unary RPC, two protobuf encodes, a Raft entry and a bbolt write per request.

## Options
A. TigerBeetle batch log plus epoch rotation.
B. New store on go.etcd.io/raft: batching, in-memory index, append-only value log, no bbolt, no MVCC copies in a B+tree.
C. Fork etcd and optimize the measured hot spots (request path allocations, double encoding, apply, bbolt), keep everything else and all of etcd's tests.

## Recommendation
See the owner round.

title: Single region or wide-area clusters
body:
Part of [Map: tigerstore, a faster etcd for Kubernetes on TigerBeetle](https://github.com/djosh34/tigerstore/issues/1).

## Question
Must tigerstore work well with its 3 nodes spread across regions (tens of ms apart), or is one region with nodes about 1 ms apart the target?

## Context
Any store with etcd's guarantees (a write is acked only once a majority has it on disk, reads are linearizable) pays at least one round trip to the nearest majority per write, and one per linearizable read. With 70 ms between nodes, every write waits 70 ms or more. Batching and pipelining keep throughput high when many requests are in flight, but Kubernetes controllers run few workers, so their rate is workers divided by latency (for example 20 workers at 70 ms is about 285 writes/s). Xline tried a one-round-trip fast path for wide-area etcd and had to give it up to keep etcd revisions correct ([Prior art](https://github.com/djosh34/tigerstore/issues/2)). A client 70 ms away from a cluster whose nodes sit in one region only adds that client's own network delay, not consensus delay.

## Options
A. One region (nodes in separate zones, about 1 ms apart) is the target. Wide-area works but is not optimized or benchmarked.
B. Wide-area is a goal: benchmark with 70 ms added between nodes, tune timeouts for it.
C. Wide-area plus weaker but faster reads for remote nodes (serializable follower reads).

## Recommendation
A.

title: Hardware limits for an etcd-compatible store
body:
Part of [Map: tigerstore, a faster etcd for Kubernetes on TigerBeetle](https://github.com/djosh34/tigerstore/issues/1).

## Question
What are the hardware limits for an etcd-compatible store on the target machines, before writing any code?

## Context
The owner wants to start from the theoretical maximum: what the hardware allows, then how close a design can get, the way TigerBeetle reasons from disk, network and memory limits. Target machines: a GitHub Actions ubuntu-24.04-arm runner (4 CPU, 16 GB, 14 GB SSD, 3 nodes on loopback) and a typical 3-node setup (NVMe, 10 Gb/s LAN). Durability per [Consistency and durability bar](https://github.com/djosh34/tigerstore/issues/8): an ack means a quorum has the write on disk.

## Options
Not a decision. A fact for later decisions.

## Recommendation
Measure on the runner with small Go microbenchmarks (in a scratch branch, workflow on push to that branch only): fsync latency and fsyncs/s at 4 KiB to 1 MiB group sizes, sequential write bandwidth, loopback RTT and bandwidth, per-op CPU for a Go gRPC unary call with etcd's protobufs (client and server), protobuf encode and decode of a 1 KiB and 10 KiB KeyValue, insert and delete in an in-memory ordered index of 1M and 10M keys, SHA-256 and a fast hash per KiB. Then derive, per resource, the ceiling for Put, CAS Txn and Delete at 1 KiB and 10 KiB values, for both latency (single client) and throughput (many clients), for a design with leader batching, one fsync per batch, an in-memory index and a value log. State which resource bounds each case and how far etcd's measured numbers (from #26) sit below each ceiling.

title: Mass deletes in Kubernetes: where the time goes
body:
Part of [Map: tigerstore, a faster etcd for Kubernetes on TigerBeetle](https://github.com/djosh34/tigerstore/issues/1).

## Question
When Kubernetes deletes many objects (a namespace with 50k objects, DeleteCollection, the garbage collector), where does the time go, and is etcd even the bottleneck?

## Context
The owner's main irritation with etcd is slowness on many transactions, especially mass deletes. By Little's law, throughput is concurrency divided by latency. If kube-apiserver or a controller deletes objects one by one with few workers (for example the apiserver flag --delete-collection-workers, the namespace controller, the garbage collector's worker counts, finalizers, a GET plus a CAS per object), then per-write latency, not etcd's throughput, sets the speed. A faster store only helps through lower latency in that case.

## Options
Not a decision. A fact for later decisions.

## Recommendation
(1) From Kubernetes v1.37.1 source: the exact request sequence for namespace deletion, DeleteCollection and GC cascading deletes, with worker counts, flags and defaults, and how many etcd requests each object costs. (2) Measure on a GitHub Actions ubuntu-24.04-arm runner with kind: create 10k and 50k ConfigMaps in a namespace, delete the namespace, and record total time, objects/s, etcd request rate and latency, etcd and apiserver CPU. Repeat with --delete-collection-workers raised. Say plainly what limits the deletion rate.

title: Why etcd is slow: write path, design choices, profile
body:
Part of [Map: tigerstore, a faster etcd for Kubernetes on TigerBeetle](https://github.com/djosh34/tigerstore/issues/1).

## Question
Why is etcd slow, where exactly does a write spend its time, and why did etcd's designers choose what they chose?

## Context
etcd already is a leader with passive followers and batches Raft entries (one WAL fsync per Ready batch, pipelined appends). Yet published throughput tops out around 50k writes/s, apply is single-threaded, bbolt allows one writer, and operators on VMs with slow disks raise heartbeat and election timeouts (for example 1 s and 10 s) because disk latency causes leader loss. The owner believes the CPU is never the real limit and that a single-threaded core with massive batching should be far faster. Prior facts in [#4](https://github.com/djosh34/tigerstore/issues/4).

## Options
Not a decision. A fact for later decisions.

## Recommendation
Two parts. (1) From etcd source at v3.7.2 and design docs or maintainer statements: the full path of a Put and a DeleteRange from gRPC to reply, every queue, goroutine hop, fsync, bbolt commit (batch-interval, batch-limit), MVCC index and watch step; why heartbeats are delayed by disk (is sending heartbeats coupled to the WAL fsync in the raft loop?); why bbolt, why MVCC history in the backend, why the 2 GiB quota; known upstream efforts to fix these. (2) Measure on a GitHub Actions ubuntu-24.04-arm runner (3-member etcd 3.7.2 on one runner): put and delete throughput and latency at 1, 16, 256 and 1,024 clients, with CPU profiles (pprof) of the leader at saturation, and a breakdown of where CPU and wall time go (gRPC and protobuf, raft, WAL, apply, bbolt, index, GC). Say what saturates first: CPU, disk, or a serial step.

title: TigerBeetle or another log, given growth and packaging facts
body:
Part of [Map: tigerstore, a faster etcd for Kubernetes on TigerBeetle](https://github.com/djosh34/tigerstore/issues/1). Revisits [TigerBeetle: requirement or means](https://github.com/djosh34/tigerstore/issues/13) after the growth and packaging facts.

## Question
Given what we now know, is TigerBeetle still the log tigerstore is built on?

## Context
- As a key-value store TigerBeetle does not fit: no key strings, no scans, permanent records, growth of 7 to 350+ GB/day/replica at 1,000 to 5,000 nodes with one record per write ([#16](https://github.com/djosh34/tigerstore/issues/16), being measured in [#24](https://github.com/djosh34/tigerstore/issues/24)).
- In the batch-log design (being evaluated in [#14](https://github.com/djosh34/tigerstore/issues/14)) TigerBeetle only orders batch digests and fences writers. It would see a few hundred records/s, far below its capacity, so its speed is not what makes tigerstore fast. Batching, an in-memory index, a separate value log and single-threaded apply do that, and they work on any replicated log.
- Costs of TigerBeetle in that role: epoch rotation to reclaim disk, a supervised child process, io_uring (disabled by default on RHEL 9, a real drop-in hurdle), no TLS (tunnel), all 3 replicas needed for upgrades, about 2.1 GiB RAM per replica minimum, cgo client.
- Gains: VSR with years of deterministic simulation testing, strong handling of disk corruption, the owner's original thesis tested.
- Alternative: an in-process Raft library (go.etcd.io/raft, the one etcd uses), with the same batching, value log and in-memory index. Raft snapshots truncate the log, so no growth problem, no extra process, no io_uring, native mTLS.

## Options
A. Keep TigerBeetle as the requirement. Build batch log plus epoch rotation and find out.
B. Keep the log behind a tiny interface (append batch digest, tail, read barrier, fence). Build TigerBeetle first, add a Raft backend later only if numbers or operations demand it.
C. Switch to go.etcd.io/raft now. Keep the rest of the design.

## Recommendation
See the owner round.

title: Measure TigerBeetle bytes per transfer and any way to prune
body:
Part of [Map: tigerstore, a faster etcd for Kubernetes on TigerBeetle](https://github.com/djosh34/tigerstore/issues/1).

## Question
How many bytes does one TigerBeetle transfer really take on disk, and is there any way, stock or announced, to delete or archive old transfers?

## Context
[Design: TigerBeetle storage growth under k8s load](https://github.com/djosh34/tigerstore/issues/16) used an uncalibrated 1 KiB per transfer. The struct is 128 bytes; TigerBeetle's hardware guide estimates 16 TiB for 40 billion transfers (about 440 bytes). #16 also claims 0.17.9 writes a 256-byte AccountEvent for every transfer even with history off. The owner doubts the numbers and asks whether never-delete is a hard limit. The TigerBeetle "trillion transactions" post mentions an object-storage connector.

## Options
Not a decision. A fact for later decisions.

## Recommendation
Measure, do not estimate: on a GitHub Actions ubuntu-24.04-arm runner (io_uring works there; this host has it disabled, do not change host sysctls), create a 1-replica and a 3-replica cluster with 0.17.9 and the stable --cache-grid=32MiB profile, write 10 million and 50 million transfers (time-ordered ids, user_data set, two accounts), and report data-file growth per transfer after the file stops growing in chunks. Repeat with random ids. Also report bytes per account. Then answer from source and first-party posts: is the AccountEvent claim right, does any released or announced feature delete, prune or archive transfers, and what does the TigerBeetle team say about ledger growth.

title: Security of traffic between nodes
body:
Part of [Map: tigerstore, a faster etcd for Kubernetes on TigerBeetle](https://github.com/djosh34/tigerstore/issues/1).

## Question
How is traffic between the 3 nodes protected?

## Context
TigerBeetle has no authentication and no TLS. Its replica-to-replica and client traffic is plaintext on its own port. The value-store replication between tigerstore processes is our own Go code, so mTLS there is easy. etcd normally runs peer traffic over TLS, and kubeadm sets that up. Wrapping TigerBeetle's traffic in a TLS tunnel inside our binary puts an extra hop on every consensus message.

## Options
A. First release: TigerBeetle ports bind to a private node network and the docs say so. Our own peer traffic uses mTLS. Client-facing etcd API uses TLS as decided.
B. Our binary tunnels TigerBeetle traffic through mTLS.
C. Leave it to the operator (WireGuard or a private network).

## Recommendation
A. Measure the cost of B later if users ask.

B. A plus a Jepsen port.
C. Layers 1 and 3 only.

A. Unit tests and layer 1 on every PR, layer 2 and short chaos runs on every PR, full conformance and long chaos runs (for example 1 hour) nightly and before a release. A checker timeout or a skipped check counts as a failure, not a pass.

## Context

title: Design: TigerBeetle storage growth under k8s load
body:
Part of [Map: tigerstore, a faster etcd for Kubernetes on TigerBeetle](https://github.com/djosh34/tigerstore/issues/1).

## Question
Stock TigerBeetle never deletes accounts or transfers. How big does it grow under k8s load, and what keeps that bounded?

## Context
Fixed by the owner: Go, 3 nodes with one executable each, stock unpatched TigerBeetle as the only consensus, linearizable reads and writes, acked writes (value bytes included) survive loss of one node, scope is what kube-apiserver needs plus TLS, open to the full etcd v3 API later. Facts: [#3](https://github.com/djosh34/tigerstore/issues/3) lists the exact etcd subset k8s uses and TigerBeetle's primitives, [#2](https://github.com/djosh34/tigerstore/issues/2) the prior art.
k8s writes all the time: about 1 lease renewal per node every 10 s, pod status updates, events with 1 h TTL. TigerBeetle's default storage limit is 16 TiB, its guide estimates about 16 TiB for 40 billion transfers. Every etcd write becomes at least one, likely several, 128-byte transfers. Ideas to weigh: fewer transfers per write, accounts reuse, accepting growth with a documented disk budget, and epochs: periodically start a fresh TigerBeetle cluster and move only live state into it, all while serving.

## Options
To be produced by the design work.

## Recommendation
A comment with a growth model in bytes per day for clusters of 100, 1,000 and 5,000 nodes, the disk budget that implies, and each mitigation with its cost in complexity and its effect on the guarantees. Say plainly whether unbounded growth makes the design unworkable.

title: Design: durable value store that is not the bottleneck
body:
Part of [Map: tigerstore, a faster etcd for Kubernetes on TigerBeetle](https://github.com/djosh34/tigerstore/issues/1).

## Question
How are value bytes (and key bytes) made durable on a quorum without becoming the bottleneck?

## Context
Fixed by the owner: Go, 3 nodes with one executable each, stock unpatched TigerBeetle as the only consensus, linearizable reads and writes, acked writes (value bytes included) survive loss of one node, scope is what kube-apiserver needs plus TLS, open to the full etcd v3 API later. Facts: [#3](https://github.com/djosh34/tigerstore/issues/3) lists the exact etcd subset k8s uses and TigerBeetle's primitives, [#2](https://github.com/djosh34/tigerstore/issues/2) the prior art.
TigerBeetle only stores a 128-bit hash. The owner fears the value store's durability becomes the bottleneck and wants a smart design. Constraints: an acked write must survive loss of any one node of three, value bytes included. A hash committed in TigerBeetle must never point at bytes nobody has. k8s objects are mostly 1 to 20 KiB, up to 1.5 MiB. Heavy churn: node leases every 10 s, status updates, events. Ideas to weigh: content-addressed immutable blobs, write bytes to 2 of 3 nodes before committing the hash (write last, read first), group commit with one fsync per batch, an append-only value log per node (WiscKey style), pipelining the blob replication with the TigerBeetle commit, catching up a node that missed blobs, garbage collection after compaction, and whether value replication can share TigerBeetle's own batching rhythm.

## Options
To be produced by the design work.

## Recommendation
A design document as a comment: write path with its latency budget (RTTs and fsyncs per write), throughput limits per resource (disk bandwidth, fsyncs, network, CPU), failure cases (node crash mid-write, a blob on only one node, a node rejoining after hours, disk corruption), recovery, GC, and an estimate of whether this or TigerBeetle is the bottleneck on the 4 CPU, 16 GB GitHub runners and on real 3-node hardware.

title: Design: etcd semantics on stock TigerBeetle
body:
Part of [Map: tigerstore, a faster etcd for Kubernetes on TigerBeetle](https://github.com/djosh34/tigerstore/issues/1).

## Question
How do etcd's semantics map onto stock TigerBeetle plus a Go layer, exactly and provably?

## Context
Fixed by the owner: Go, 3 nodes with one executable each, stock unpatched TigerBeetle as the only consensus, linearizable reads and writes, acked writes (value bytes included) survive loss of one node, scope is what kube-apiserver needs plus TLS, open to the full etcd v3 API later. Facts: [#3](https://github.com/djosh34/tigerstore/issues/3) lists the exact etcd subset k8s uses and TigerBeetle's primitives, [#2](https://github.com/djosh34/tigerstore/issues/2) the prior art.
Open parts: what each 128-byte account and transfer holds; global revision numbering with one revision per Txn; CAS for MOD==n, MOD==0 after delete and recreate, and VERSION==n; returning the failed branch's value at the Txn's read point; ambiguous retries after a timeout; the ordered key index (TigerBeetle has no key strings or prefix scans); linearizable reads (read barrier against TigerBeetle); watch with prevKV, progress notifications and RequestProgress (CDC, GetChangeEvents or query_transfers polling); LeaseGrant and TTL expiry; Compact; node restart and catch-up. Hashing keys into 128-bit ids needs a collision story.

## Options
To be produced by the design work: at least two complete designs with their trade-offs.

## Recommendation
A design document as a comment: record layouts, the write path and read path step by step, the invariants, and a short argument for why each etcd guarantee holds, including under crashes and retries. Name every open risk and the cheapest experiment that settles it.

title: TigerBeetle: requirement or means
body:
Part of [Map: tigerstore, a faster etcd for Kubernetes on TigerBeetle](https://github.com/djosh34/tigerstore/issues/1).

## Question
Is TigerBeetle a requirement, or the means to a faster etcd?

## Context
Your premise is that etcd is slow because of coordination between machines. etcd (Raft) and TigerBeetle (VSR) both run one primary and replicate each write to a quorum before acking, so per write they coordinate about the same. TigerBeetle's speed comes from batching thousands of fixed 128-byte records per request, io_uring, static memory and a tight single-threaded state machine. TigerBeetle stores no key strings, has no ordered range scans and, as far as known, never deletes transfers. So the ordered key index, watch and compaction would live in tigerstore, rebuilt from TigerBeetle's log. The research in [etcd semantics k8s needs vs TigerBeetle primitives](https://github.com/djosh34/tigerstore/issues/3) and [Prior art](https://github.com/djosh34/tigerstore/issues/2) will show how much TigerBeetle actually gives.

## Options
A. TigerBeetle is a requirement. The project is "etcd on TigerBeetle" or nothing.
B. TigerBeetle is the first candidate for the replicated log. If research or the spike shows it does not fit, the plan may pick another log with the same single-threaded, batched design.
C. Drop TigerBeetle now and design the log from scratch.

## Recommendation
B. The goal you stated is a faster etcd. Keep TigerBeetle as the bet, but let the facts decide.

title: Deployment shape
body:
Part of [Map: tigerstore, a faster etcd for Kubernetes on TigerBeetle](https://github.com/djosh34/tigerstore/issues/1).

## Question
What does an operator deploy?

## Context
etcd is one binary per node, usually 3 nodes. The idea here has three parts: TigerBeetle replicas, the etcd-API server, and the value store. TigerBeetle runs as its own process and supports specific cluster sizes (to be confirmed in [etcd semantics k8s needs vs TigerBeetle primitives](https://github.com/djosh34/tigerstore/issues/3)).

## Options
A. Same footprint as etcd: 3 nodes, each running one TigerBeetle replica and one tigerstore process that serves the etcd API and stores value bytes.
B. Separate tiers: a TigerBeetle cluster, stateless etcd-API servers, and value-store nodes, each scaled on its own.
C. A. by default, with tiers that can be split later.

A. Same machines as etcd makes the benchmark fair and the swap a real drop-in. Splitting tiers is a later concern.

title: Judge for faster than etcd
body:
Part of [Map: tigerstore, a faster etcd for Kubernetes on TigerBeetle](https://github.com/djosh34/tigerstore/issues/1).

## Question
What is the judge for "faster than etcd"?

## Context
You named max object count and max write throughput first, latency second. There are two levels to measure. At the etcd API level, etcd's own benchmark tool drives put, range and txn directly. At the Kubernetes level, clusterloader2 or kube-burner drive a real apiserver, where the apiserver itself may become the limit. Target numbers wait on [Where etcd's limits are and how to benchmark against it](https://github.com/djosh34/tigerstore/issues/4).

## Options
A. etcd API level only.
B. Kubernetes level only.
C. Both: the etcd API level decides the kill criterion and the claims, the Kubernetes level proves real gain and no regression.

## Recommendation
C. Same hardware, same replica count (3), same durability, both stores tuned per their own docs.

title: Implementation language
body:
Part of [Map: tigerstore, a faster etcd for Kubernetes on TigerBeetle](https://github.com/djosh34/tigerstore/issues/1).

## Question
Which language is tigerstore written in?

## Context
etcd, kine and Kubernetes are Go, and the etcd protobufs and server stubs can be reused from Go. TigerBeetle is Zig and ships official clients; a Go client is expected, to be confirmed in [etcd semantics k8s needs vs TigerBeetle primitives](https://github.com/djosh34/tigerstore/issues/3). Rust and Zig give tighter control of memory, at the cost of rewriting the gRPC and etcd protocol layer. Go is installed on this host, Zig is not.

## Options
A. Go.
B. Rust.
C. Zig.

## Recommendation
A. Go. The heavy lifting is in TigerBeetle, and Go reuses etcd's own API types and test tooling.

title: Consistency and durability bar
body:
Part of [Map: tigerstore, a faster etcd for Kubernetes on TigerBeetle](https://github.com/djosh34/tigerstore/issues/1).

## Question
What consistency and durability must tigerstore keep?

## Context
etcd is linearizable and durable: a write is acked only after a quorum has it on disk. Some fast etcd replacements drop this (k8s-1m's mem_etcd keeps state in memory, to be confirmed in [Prior art](https://github.com/djosh34/tigerstore/issues/2)). The chaos tests you want only mean something if there is a guarantee to check.

## Options
A. Same as etcd: linearizable reads and writes, acked writes survive loss of a minority of nodes, including value bytes.
B. Linearizable writes, but reads may be stale by a bounded time.
C. Durability relaxed for speed (ack before fsync).

## Recommendation
A. Anything weaker is not a drop-in replacement, and the benchmark would not be a fair fight.

title: Compatibility scope of the drop-in
body:
Part of [Map: tigerstore, a faster etcd for Kubernetes on TigerBeetle](https://github.com/djosh34/tigerstore/issues/1).

## Question
What does "drop-in replacement for etcd" cover?

## Context
kube-apiserver uses a small part of etcd v3 (see [etcd semantics k8s needs vs TigerBeetle primitives](https://github.com/djosh34/tigerstore/issues/3)). Full etcd v3 also has auth and RBAC, cluster membership, maintenance (defrag, snapshot, alarms), the v3 lock and election APIs, gRPC gateway, and etcdctl expectations. kine took the k8s-only route.

## Options
A. Exactly what kube-apiserver needs, plus health and the etcdctl commands an operator uses for debugging (get, put, del, watch, endpoint status).
B. A. plus TLS client certificates (kubeadm and most installs require them).
C. Full etcd v3 API.

## Recommendation
B. k8s plus TLS. Full etcd v3 is a separate product and adds nothing to the speed claim.

title: etcd semantics k8s needs vs TigerBeetle primitives
body:
Part of [Map: tigerstore, a faster etcd for Kubernetes on TigerBeetle](https://github.com/djosh34/tigerstore/issues/1).

## Question
Which etcd semantics does kube-apiserver depend on, and which of them can TigerBeetle express directly?

## Context
kube-apiserver uses a subset of etcd v3: Range with prefix, limit and continuation, Txn with compare on mod_revision, Put and Delete, Watch from a revision with prevKV and progress notifications, Compact, leases with TTL, and the current revision in response headers. kine documents the subset it implements. TigerBeetle stores fixed 128-byte accounts and transfers with 128-bit ids and a few user_data fields, has linked (atomic) chains, unique ids, balance limits, pending transfers with timeouts, query_transfers and query_accounts, cluster timestamps, and possibly change data capture. Transfers appear to be immutable and never deleted.

## Options
Not a decision. A fact for later decisions.

## Recommendation
Answer with sources: (1) the exact etcd API subset kube-apiserver uses in current Kubernetes (check kine and k8s.io/apiserver storage/etcd3). (2) For each item, whether TigerBeetle can do it directly, with a trick (for example CAS through unique transfer ids), or not at all. (3) TigerBeetle facts: throughput numbers and batch sizes, cluster sizes, client languages (Go?), aarch64 and io_uring needs, data file size limits, deletion and history retention, CDC, license, release cadence and upgrade rules.

For each project: design, numbers it claims, k8s compatibility level (conformance?), what broke or stayed limited, maintenance status, primary source links.

title: Map: tigerstore, a faster etcd for Kubernetes
body:
## Destination
A full autonomous plan that builds tigerstore, a drop-in etcd replacement for Kubernetes: same etcd API, consensus with go.etcd.io/raft, fully new custom storage designed from what one CPU core can do at most. It passes strong e2e, deterministic simulation and chaos tests, and beats etcd on max object count and max write throughput with similar or lower latency.

## Notes
- Domain: etcd v3 API as used by kube-apiserver, go.etcd.io/raft, custom storage engine, deterministic simulation testing, linearizability and chaos testing.
- Owner's main goal: a k8s-compatible etcd replacement that is faster and holds more objects, proven by e2e and chaos tests (packet loss, corruption, delay, latency, partitions).
- The owner decides, agents find facts.
- Owner instruction, round 6: the plan runs fully autonomous while the owner is away. Keep it small and under-specified. The design may change during the plan. Hard instruction: make it wicked fast, think outside the box, do crazy things, boil the ocean. Test it brutally and try to break it, not kindly.
- Every question is a sub-issue labelled wayfinder:<type> with question, context, options and recommendation. A decision ticket closes with an "Owner answer, round N" comment, a research ticket with its answer as a comment.
- Host facts: aarch64, 8 cores, 11 GB RAM, Go 1.27.2, 45 GB free on / and 65 GB on the work mount. docker, podman, kind, kubectl, go, etcd and tc are installed. The repo is public.
- Writing follows unslop.

## Decisions so far
